Title: Improving the Physical Layout of Merchandise in Warehouses
Abstract: Do you want to know how to reduce substantially the materials-handling costs in warehouses? This article—involving a linear-programing model — provides useful guidelines for more optimal arrangements of merchandise in typical warehouses, both in the reserve and the assembly sections.

Title: Obtaining Maximum Volume from New Gasoline Outlets
Abstract: Where should a gasoline marketer build new stations? In markets where his brand is well represented, or in markets where he has a small share of the stations? The conclusions in this study will surprise many marketers, and may well be applicable to products and services other than gasoline.

Title: A Fresh Look at Franchising
Abstract: This is a timely discussion of the history, current trends, and future of franchising in one short article.

Title: The “Census” of Business: Some Contrary Evidence
Abstract: Have you ever questioned the accuracy of the U.S. Census of Business? How precise are the tabulations of the number of retail establishments in a given area at a particular time? This article compares Census data with independent sources of data, discusses the discrepancies, and offers suggestions for improving the Census of Business.

Title: Acquisitions: Another Viewpoint
Abstract: This article explores and describes two separate aspects of acquisition and merger activity: (1) the attributes of those firms considered for acquisition by major manufacturers, and (2) the changes in operations of acquired firms instituted by acquiring firms. Although the data are restricted to activities among grocery manufacturers, these manufacturers represent some of the most sagacious competitors in the entire consumer goods area. The data were gathered while the author was a staff member of the National Commission on Food Marketing.

Title: Are Your Messages Getting Through?
Abstract: What happens to an advertising or sales message after it has been received by the consumer? Findings from a number of studies are reviewed in this article to show that sales messages have a considerable chance of being blocked, modified, or of having no direct motivating effect. Some significant elements of the communication process and forces operating to block mass media messages are explained.

Title: The Promise of Simulation in Marketing
Abstract: In recognition of simulation's potential, the author was invited to speak at a meeting of the American Marketing Association on the role of simulation in marketing. For that talk an intensive survey was made of the published literature. This article presents some of the results of the survey.

Title: Planning Tomorrow Today through Successive Focusing
Abstract: Techniques for product planning are legion; but an integrated method, embracing an infinite variety of situations, has yet to be devised. The author of this article attempts this by introducing the concept of the dynamic product area, which does more than answer the traditional question: “What business are we in?”

Title: Trends and Innovations in the Marketing of Insurance
Abstract: What's happening in insurance marketing today? The gigantic institution of insurance has long been accused of conservatism, but evidence today points toward an awakened and dynamic era of change for the insurance business. Traditional marketing channels are being reappraised, and the predominant agency systems are being modified at the same time that innovations in direct-selling systems and group methods of marketing are appearing. Product diversification, automation, and other trends are noted. What these trends are, where they have come from, and how they may affect the future are explored in this article.

Title: The Automobile Buyer after the Purchase
Abstract: Customer satisfaction after the purchase is a key factor in brand loyalty. Marketing managers are becoming keenly interested in how a new purchaser feels after buying. In this study, an analysis is made of how a new car buyer feels about his purchase after it is completed. What factors determine the reactions of a customer when he begins living with his new car? This article explores the effect of customers’ personalities in relation to salesmen's persuasion attempts upon consumers’ post-purchase satisfaction.

Title: From the Editor
Marketing and the Controversy over Conglomerate Mergers
Abstract: Conglomerate mergers are the most prevalent and the most controversial of the three types of mergers—horizontal, vertical, and conglomerate. The controversy stems in part from the marketing possibilities inherent in some conglomerate mergers, but it also stems, unfortunately, from basic misconceptions of the meaning of these mergers. The present article, based on an analysis of conglomerate mergers in the history of the 1950 Amendment to Section 7 of the Clayton Act, indicates the nature and origin of the disagreement on the meaning. The author presents criteria for determining when a merger is, in part or whole, a conglomerate merger.

Title: Markets behind the Iron Curtain
Abstract: This article contains information about marketing to countries behind the Iron Curtain. Drawing on his international marketing research experience, the author indicates that many Western businessmen have tried to build trade relations with Eastbloc countries and have failed. Firms have offered merchandise they knew was needed in the Communist countries, but were unable to sell it despite its being of excellent quality, fairly priced, and adapted to the needs of these countries. The author explains why these firms were not able to sell their products and offers suggestions for successful selling to the East.

Title: What Effect Will the “Fair Packaging and Labeling Act” Have on Marketing Practices?
Affiliations: Director of Marketing Research Oscar Mayer & Co. Madison, Wisconsin
Abstract: THE Fair Packaging and Labeling Act (Public Law 89-755) will take effect July 1, 1967 (with the possibility of a 12-month postponement for individual product categories, if the federal agencies involved find such delay to be in the public interest). Marketing people will have to become familiar with the major provisions and implications of this act. Some background information on the act, popularly known as the Hart Act, is included in this article.

Title: The Role of Marketing in Israel
Abstract: In very few developing economies is the significance of the marketing function truly appreciated. Although marketing has evolved more rapidly in Israel than in most other developing nations, the marketing function is still perceived principally as selling. The author of this article explains why.

Title: Consumer Protection Via Increased Information
Abstract: Will “truth-in-packaging” lead to “truth-in-advertising”? Will “full disclosure” blossom without legislative nourishment? Are demands for consumer protection a political sham? The author discusses the trend of present consumer-protection efforts and takes a controversial position.

Title: What Is Wrong with Test Marketing?
Abstract: The testing of marketing innovations by actually placing them in a limited number of test markets and then observing consumer reaction has become a way of life for most consumer packaged-goods companies. But this writer points out that this is a much less rewarding method than if several shibboleths concerning test marketing were laid aside.

Title: The Real Challenge of Food Discounters
Abstract: How do discount food stores compare with conventional supermarkets? Can they underprice and still operate profitably? Are they able to reduce operating expenses? Is the food discounter a threat to the conventional supermarket? This article provides some insights into these questions based upon the practices of three noncompeting companies engaged in both conventional supermarket and discount food operations. The author also reports the actual operating figures of comparable discount and conventional outlets.

Title: The Integrated Management Approach to Marketing
Abstract: The basic objectives of the business firm cannot be optimized by internal departmental planning, says this author. He argues that the satisfaction of departmental goals too frequently conflicts with other departmental goals and company objectives. Optimum interdepartmental planning is called INTEGRATED MANAGEMENT and training in this area is greatly needed in modern schools of business.

Title: Aerospace Discovers Marketing
Abstract: Executives in the aerospace industry are re-evaluating their attitudes toward marketing; and emphasis is being shifted from engineering and accounting skills to marketing. The author, a marketing consultant to the aerospace industry, shows how and why this new emphasis is important both to the firm and to the customer.

Title: Measuring Language Difficulty in Advertising Copy
Abstract: How well an advertisement is understood by its readers, viewers, or listeners is a very important measure of its efficacy. In this article the author presents a number of methods for measuring difficulty of language, and thus comprehensibility, of advertising. He shows how “desk-research” and “field-research” findings are applicable to all forms of written and verbal communication, including advertising.

Title: Communications and Industrial Selling
Abstract: This article reports on research that investigated the relative importance of company reputation, salesman effort, and sales-message quality in industrial selling. It distinguishes between the relative importance of “high risk” and “low risk” purchasing situations, between “high-competence” (well-informed) and “low-competence” purchasers, and between the immediate effects of a sales presentation and the abiding effects. And it evaluates differences in sales effectiveness between the “quality” of a salesman's presentation, his familiarity with the product, and how honest his prospects think he is.

Title: Positive Robinson-Patman Pricing
Authors: Charles C. Slater, Frank H. Mossman
Abstract: Do present interpretations of the Robinson-Patman Act cause sellers to discriminate against large customers? This article deals with a new computer-based analysis procedure for improvement in consistency and reduction in discrimination in pricing practices. The authors show the steps needed to develop computer-based, marketing-oriented cost accounting systems and the application of this new pricing practice to an actual business situation.

Title: Commentary on “Impact of Government upon the Market System”
Abstract: powerful enterprises. Thus, there is the special Small Business Administration in the federal government dedicated to the interests of small business. Thus, too, the Supreme Court of the United States in recent decisions, especially Brown Shoe, has made the preservation of viable small business a standard of action superior both to efficiency and the mainteance of competition in an abstract sense. Conversely, powerful well-established corporations find it increasingly difficult to grow by the simple processes of acquisition or merger. The enforcement of the revised 1950 Section 7 of the Clayton Act is increasingly affecting the opportunities of growth by acquisition. Consequently, large enterprises are forced increasingly to plan growth through internal expansion-horizontally, vertically, functionally, and through conglomerate diversification. Possibly in the near future such avenues of internal growth may be under increasing questioning. Finally, the weight and specific character of taxes affect growth plans and opportunities.

Title: Impact of Government upon the Market System
Authors: E. T. Grether, Robert J. Holloway
Abstract: Suggestions are presented for research on the impact of governmental policies, programs, and regulations upon the functioning of the market system as a whole, and upon specific subsystems. The authors point out that intervention by government at all levels is one of the two most significant environmental forces affecting marketing. This paper is the first of four reports developed by the AMA Task Force on Research on Basic Problems in Marketing, chaired by Donald R. Longman. The other papers will be presented in subsequent issues of the JOURNAL OF MARKETING. Each paper will be accompanied by a review by Seymour Banks, in which the issues involved in each paper will be highlighted and the various papers related to one another.

Title: A Fond Farewell to the “Journal of Marketing”
Affiliations: Northwestern University—serving, School of Business, Advertising in the Medill School of Journalism
Abstract: Last July the Editor of the Journal of Marketing submitted his resignation, to become effective at the end of 1966. This is his message of appreciation to the scores of marketing executives and marketing professors who have worked with him in the development of the publication.

Title: The Danger of “Local” International Advertising
Abstract: Marketers cannot ignore nationalistic tendencies and other hidden hazards in international advertising. But universal advertising appeals, communicated in the local idiom, can be more effective than is generally realized, argues a top advertising executive.

Title: Measuring Change in the Advertising Agency Business
Authors: John J. Humpal, Henry G. Meyer-Oertel
Affiliations: University of Chicago's Graduate School of Business; National Register Publishing Co., Inc.
Abstract: There is a general impression of extreme volatility in the advertising agency business … but how accurate is this impression? This is a report on account-switching and personnel changes in agencies during a I-year period.

Title: Educating Men for International Marketing
Authors: Y. Hugh Furuhashi, Harry F. Evarts
Affiliations: Notre Dame University; Dean of the College of Business Administration at Ohio University
Abstract: Persons specializing in international marketing ought to be educated for the jobs they are to do. The question is—how should they be educated for these positions? The authors, who began this article as a result of a Workshop on International Business at the New York University in 1964, give some useful answers.

Title: Is Communications Research Really Worthwhile?
Affiliations: Doyle Dane Bernbach, Inc., New York
Abstract: The author of this article questions many of the accepted “principles” derived from experimental studies in the field of communications research. But he also proposes some basic conclusions for the field of marketing.

Title: The Merchandising Decision under Uncertainty
Abstract: Retailing institutions have become enormous, complex operations. One result has been an increasing tendency to turn toward quantitative techniques and models as a means of helping the merchant solve many of the problems that arise. This article shows how the Bayesian model can be applied to merchandising.

Title: An experiment on Consumer Dissonance
Abstract: In this article the author describes a consumer-decision experiment which involved four dissonant-producing factors simultaneously. Even though the study is limited to only one product, an automobile battery, the findings provide useful insights that might be applicable to various product categories.

Title: Private-label Marketing in the ice-cream Industry
Authors: William H. Kaven, David L. Call
Affiliations: Cornell University, University of Virginia; Graduate School of Nutrition, Cornell University
Abstract: The growth of private-label products in the retail grocery industry has made an impact on manufacturers who sell both private-label and manufacturer-advertised goods. This article probes some of the problems of the ice-cream manufacturer who supplies bothlabelssimultaneously to corporate grocery chains and also to groups of affiliated independent grocers.

Title: Markup in Department Store Management
Abstract: The author holds that markup percentage can make substantial contributions to the department store as a negotiation tool, as a control and planning device, and as a decision tool.

Title: Standard Classification of Consumer Characteristics
Affiliations: Center for Advanced Practice, McCann Erickson, Inc., New York.
Abstract: Here is an opportunity to find out about the history and also the potential benefits of standardized classifications of respondents in consumer surveys.

Title: A Model for Ethics in Marketing
Abstract: Is a given marketing action always ethical, never ethical, or ethical relative to time, place, and circumstances? Upon what logical bases can a marketer determine what is “right” for him to do, not only in domestic but also in international business? This article presents a schematic plan for analyzing the variables inherent in the ethics of decision-making; and a framework for social and personal ethics is proposed.

Title: The Process of Innovation and the Diffusion of Innovation
Affiliations: University of California at Los Angeles
Abstract: “Innovate or Perish” is the marketer's cry of the 1960s. And “Perish as You Innovate” could well be the marketing slogan of the 1970s. But several questions arise. Can innovation be programed to occur? What is the nature of the diffusion process? Can consumer “innovators” be identified and appealed to? How do advertising and personal influence compare in effectiveness for new product diffusion? Here are some answers to these questions.

Title: Marketing Management Concepts Yesterday and Today
Authors: Bernard J. La Londe, Edward J. Morrison
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration, Michigan State University; University of Colorado
Abstract: In this historical note we find a direct application of Frederick W. Taylor's scientific management concepts to early sales management, scientific marketing management, and modem marketing management. The authors of this article review the applications of scientific management to marketing during the period from approximately World War I to the depression of the early 1930s, and they show how the first large-scale application of management concepts came about.

Title: Marketing and the United States Supreme Court
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Business Administration at The Colorado College
Abstract: When the United States Supreme Court acts to decide business controversies, how should modern marketers respond? What organizational or operational changes should management consider to conform to the decisions handed down by the Supreme Court? This article, premised on the conviction that the modern economy is constantly being modified by our legal institutions, analyzes eight different decisions handed down by the Supreme Court during 1965, as well as appropriate responses for marketers.

Title: Would you Want your Daughter to Marry a Marketing Man?
Abstract: The author of this article is not angry. But he is deadly serious in questioning the significance of much of modern marketing. He believes that many aspects of the field of marketing are both irrelevant and unethical. Is he right or wrong?

During high-school and college days Wendell Smith learned retailing at the grassroots level by selling in the family shoe store in Shenandoah, Iowa. Upon graduation from the State University of Iowa in 1932, the 21-year-old Smith worked in the family business for another two years, except for a brief interlude as a trainee with the Florsheim Shoe Company in Chicago. What Kind of Corporate Objectives?
Authors: Harper W. Boyd, Sidney J. Levy
Affiliations: Stanford University Graduate School of Business.; Northwestern University School of Business and a Consultant to Social Research, Inc.
Abstract: What are the most effective ways of devising overall corporate objectives? Here are analyses of six different categories of marketing objectives, especially useful to top management.

Title: Prepurchase Behavior of Buyers of Small Electrical Appliances
Affiliations: Cornell University Graduate School of Business and Public Administration.
Abstract: American consumers purchase over $400 billion of goods and services each year; and numerous investigations of their purchasing behavior have concentrated on patterns of store visitations. This article emphasizes the role of other sources of information in the selection of small electrical appliances by Christmas shoppers.

Title: Behavior Patterns of Supermarket Shoppers
Abstract: What are the reasons for the decline in supermarket shopping-loyalty during the past decade? What is behind the trend toward more frequent shopping by supermarket customers? Why is readership of food store advertising in newspapers increasing? How accurate is the prediction of credit purchasing of food in supermarkets? Is interest in saving trading stamps on the wane? How does discount store food shopping differ from shopping in conventional supermarkets? The answers to these questions should be of interest to all marketers.

Title: Guidelines for a Store-location Strategy Study
Affiliations: Lecturer on Food Distribution and Comparative Marketing the Harvard Business School.
Abstract: The large investments in modern store facilities and the long lease commitments make it necessary for retailing firms and for shopping-center developers to employ store-location research. In this article the author presents 16 fundamental steps or guidelines, distilled from 35 years of experience, for planning and executing comprehensive store - location studies. These guidelines are of interest not only to marketing research specialists, but also to business administrators who must make store-location expansion decisions.

Title: A Missing Link in Physical Distribution System Design
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration, Harvard University.
Abstract: Spatial concepts of system design have outlived their usefulness, says the author of this article. He holds that a more useful framework for future analysis can be based on temporal measures—that it offers the opportunity to develop an analytic approach devoid of crippling assumptions.

Title: What is Meant by Services?
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business and Public Administration, Cornell University.
Abstract: The marketing discipline has been concerned primarily with GOODS. Yet SERVICES are claiming an increasing share of the consumer's dollar. This author argues that marketing people should direct more of their attention to the services sector. What are the marketing characteristics of services? Are goods solely goods—services solely services? Is not the marketing of services by government agencies an appropriate province for marketing analysis? These are some of the questions considered here.

Title: A New Approach to Test Marketing
Abstract: Today's test markets are a surprisingly obsolete management tool, says the author of this article. Their ability to predict ultimate success is proving to be both limited and questionable. Yet the limitations of traditional test marketing conflict with the growing need for greater predictive precision than ever before. This article indicates what the future may be for test markets.

Title: Dissecting the Segmentation Syndrome
Affiliations: R. O. Loen Company, Management Consultants, and a Vice President of Loen, Brandt & Company in Palo Alto, California.
Abstract: If there were but 500,000 potential customers for a given product in the world and a decision of how much to spend on wooing each of them had to be made, upon what basis would the decision be made? Once upon a time a measurement of their relative needs or abilities to buy provided a satisfactory guidepost for the decision. But today there are other factors that must be considered. In this article the author traces how such decisions have been made in the past. He then proposes a method of market segmentation that will be of interest to marketers in both large and small firms.

Title: Does Advertising Belong in the Capital Budget?
Abstract: Whether advertising is an investment and so should be treated like other parts of the capital budget is a question of moment to marketing managers. Viewing promotion as an investment could bring dramatic changes in decision-making, market-testing, measurements of effectiveness, and value judgments that are required in determining how much to spend on promotion. The economic case for an investment approach to the advertising budget is the theme of this article by a distinguished economist.

Title: Marketing's Role in the Change to the Metric System
Affiliations: Market Development, General Electric Company, Louisville, Kentucky.
Abstract: Practically all the nations of the world use the metric system of weights and measures. Yet the United States continues to offer goods, produced according to nonmetric standards, in the world markets in competition with metric products from other countries. The marketing aspects of the metric problem are now more important than ever: efforts to increase export trade; Britain's decision to move to the metric system; and widespread utilization of electronic data processing equipment, which uses the decimal system in calculations.

Title: Marketing in the Iron Curtain Countries
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Transportation Administration, Graduate School of Business, Michigan State University.
Abstract: What are the implications of a shift in the Iron Curtain countries toward marketing? How will they affect marketing functions and institutions? The author shows the weaknesses in the existing planned systems, and he charts the future of what may develop.

Title: The Refounding Process in Business
Affiliations: Paul V. Galvin, founder of Motorola Inc., who died in 1959.
Abstract: When a company takes on a change in targets, a change in the markets it satisfies, or a change in products, that triggers the re-founding process — a more complex process than the typical process called growth. And marketers can find an exciting challenge in this refounding process.

Legal Developments in Marketing
Peter G. Peterson
Affiliations: Department of Marketing University of Illinois at Chicago Circle
Abstract: The business philosophy variously known as the Marketing Concept or the Total Marketing Approach has now been on the American scene for more than a decade. It is only natural that its advocates should look for signs indicating its general adoption by progressive business firms. One proof might exist in the gravitation of corporate leadership into the hands of men whose early business experience was in the marketing arena. Logically, such men should be consumer-oriented rather than production-minded, should be knowledgeable in the area of consumer behavior, and should believe that marketing distinguishes business from other institutions in our society. The career of Peter G. Peterson, President of Bell & Howell, manufacturers of high-quality photographic products, electronic instruments, and business equipment, provides an outstanding case example. Before assuming the broadPETER G er responsibilities of corporate leadership, Mr. Peterson spent ten years performing a variety of marketing jobs. Born in Kearney, Nebraska, in 1926, he was graduated summa cum laude with a B.S. degree from Northwestern University in 1947. His first job was as a market analyst for Market Facts, Inc., Chicago-based research firm. The pattern for his rapid progression through executive positions was set early, for he was appointed Associate Director of the firm in 1949 and Executive Vice President in 1952. Along the way Peterson obtained an M.B.A. degree with honors, granted by the University of Chicago in 1951.

Title: What Time Allocation is Most Productive for Sales Managers?
Affiliations: Marketing Research Oscar Mayer & Co. Madison, Wisconsin

Title: Keeping Pace with the Computer Age
Effects of a Newspaper Strike on Retail Sales
Affiliations: Department of the University of Detroit, and a Consultant to the Research Department of the J. Walter Thompson Company, Detroit.
Abstract: What are the effects on retail sales of a newspaper strike? This article discusses the sales effects of the 134-day Detroit newspaper strike of 1964, with respect to the various cities within the Detroit Metropolitan Area. This case history leads to some interesting hypotheses as to the effects of newspaper strikes on individual consumers and retailers.

Title: Are Consumer Grades Needed?
Affiliations: Head of Family Economics at Kansas State University. Iowa State University and Florida State University.
Abstract: Are consumer grades justified? If so, what types? The author builds his case at several levels. Do his arguments indicate the need for any type of action, either by business or by government?

Title: Competitive Oligopolistic Pricing
Affiliations: Economics, College of Business Administration, Arizona State University. College of William and Mary.
Abstract: Do oligopolistic industries evolve a pricing pattern which is inimical to consumer welfare? In this article, pricing policies in a major American industry are examined in the light of orthodox analysis. The results shed some light on the relevance of oligopolistic pricing theory in judging the competitiveness of certain industrial markets.

Title: The Environment for Marketing in Peru
Abstract: The “environmental view” of marketing focuses on the basic forces—such as economic, social, cultural and geographical — which give shape and direction to any macro marketing system. The author uses Peru as a “case study,” to show how environmental factors give rise to marketing and consumption characteristics and thus permit meaningful between-country comparisons.

Title: Retailing Evolution or Revolution in Chile?
Affiliations: The Pennsylvania State University. The University of Texas.
Abstract: The incipient Chilean supermarket industry faces formidable barriers in attempting to replace the traditional food retailing structure. The author of this article examines the present state of the shift to modern retailing methods, the desirability of that shift, the barriers it faces, and the position of the government in deciding whether the change will be evolutionary or revolutionary.

Title: Education for Marketing in the 1970s
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Michigan State University. University of Manitoba, an M.B.A. from the University of Chicago, The Ohio State University.
Abstract: What is the future of marketing education in the 1970s? The answers given here are important both for teachers and practitioners of marketing. This article is based on an address given at the annual meeting of the American Association of Collegiate Schools of Business in late 1965.

Title: A Forward Step in Performance Evaluation
Affiliations: Columbia University's Graduate School of Business.
Abstract: Persons responsible for evaluation of performance have found that use of single-criterion measures invariably leads to undesirable side-effects. As a remedy, designers of evaluation methods would like to use multiple in place of single criteria, but are likely to have difficulty in amalgamating their multiple measures into a meaningful whole. Here is a method for combining multiple-criterion scores into a conceptually satisfying, overall figure-of-merit which can be used to rank subjects or projects in order of their excellence.

Title: The Strategy Selection Chart
Affiliations: University of Illinois, Northwestern Graduate School of Business Administration in 1964.
Abstract: How to stimulate or expand selective demand and establish product distinctiveness is a major concern of most marketers today. The Strategy Selection Chart provides a tentative solution to this problem, although of course subject to individual interpretation. The chart is valuable in presenting a conceptual view of the process of strategy selection within a framework of product differentiation versus market segmentation.

Title: What is a Market?
Affiliations: The Medill School of Journalism of Northwestern University. Northwestern in 1957, and has been on the teaching staff since 1953.
Abstract: Markets are people. But what kind of people? Traditional demographic methods of classifying people into markets have lost much of their ability to discriminate prospects from non-prospects or poor from good prospects. This article brings many of the traditional as well as newer methods of market definitions together into a conceptual whole.

Title: A Perfect Measurement of Advertising's Contribution to Marketing
Abstract: The author of this article is very sympathetic with the views of all advertisers who want to know what they are “getting” for their investment in advertising. But he is also frustrated, because he does not know the answer … and he does not think anyone else does. In fact, he is so frustrated that he proposes a “perfect measurement” of advertising's contribution to marketing.

Title: What Are the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Marketing Executives?
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business at Indiana University.
Abstract: Traditional ways of framing questions about the social and ethical responsibilities of marketing have on the whole been self-defeating. In fact, the discovery of workable answers to the question, “What are the social responsibilities of marketing?”, is quite unlikely. Is there a better way to proceed? YES. This article shows how marketing executives can develop some operational guides, even though not universal answers.

Title: The Marketing-Accounting Partnership in Business
Affiliations: The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company. A graduate of the University of Akron, and Finance at this institution.
Abstract: The computer age has brought with it the need for increased teamwork on the part of all segments of the business enterprise. This is why the author of this article argues for close relationships between the marketing and accounting functions.

Title: The Care and Feeding of Marketing Consultants
Affiliations: Wood Products Group, Weyerhaeuser Company. Formerly he was on the staff of the Economics Department of Battelle Memorial Institute, Columbus, Ohio
Abstract: There is a way to use competent outside consulting services. There is a way to discriminate between those who are competent and those who are not. There is a way for management to utilize outside contributions without ever abdicating its own responsibilities. These are important considerations. But what if management responsibilities are abdicated and management thinks that in a consultant it has found a “crutch”? Here is a realistic diagnosis of the question.

Title: Marketing Snags and Fallacies
Affiliations: Leo Burnett Company advertising agency of Chicago
Abstract: This article is based on an address by Leo Burnett, head of one of the largest advertising agencies, when he was named 1966 Marketing Man of the Year by the Chicago Chapter of the American Marketing Association. Mr. Burnett feels that marketing men are handicapped by five major fallacies. But he points with pride as well as views with alarm — he has some constructive suggestions for the field of marketing.

Title: Theory or Research for the Marketing Decision-maker?
Affiliations: Board of Market Facts, Inc. Market Facts ROC International
Abstract: Marketing theorists and marketing men in business view each other with mild suspicion, neither fully recognizing that the activities of both groups are aimed at improving the decision-making process. The author of this article holds that marketing research is more useful than marketing theory in the selection of the most appropriate course of marketing action. He believes that the most fruitful opportunities for the marketing theorist are in the development of theory for improving the design of marketing research activity.

Title: Improved Forecasting through Feedback
Affiliations: Los Angeles Center, Computer Applications, Inc., Los Angeles, University of California at Los Angeles.
Abstract: Feedback is essential to modern control — we could not get a rocket to the moon without it. And what is useful for the scientific world also holds true for the managerial world. Can techniques of feedback be applied to improved forecasting of costs over the fiscal year, or to improved forecasting of contractual commitments? This article develops the basis for feedback forecasting, as well as the establishment of control limits for determining which forecasts depart significantly from plan.

Title: A Profit-oriented Decision System
Abstract: As marketing activities have grown more complex, it has become difficult to relate individual marketing decisions to the basic profit objective. This article presents a Profit-Oriented Decision (PROD) system to solve this problem for a wide variety of marketing decisions.

Title: Patterns of Media-audience Accumulation
Affiliations: Reach, McClinton & Co., Inc., New York
Abstract: Are there predictable patterns of media-audience accumulations over time? Do they differ from one medium to the next, or between types of activity within a given medium? The author explores some of the facts, makes some inferences, and indicates how to broaden the current body of knowledge in this important area.

Title: A New Technique to Analyze Tourist Markets
Affiliations: Southern California Laboratories of Stanford Research Institute, Bureau of Business Research at the University of Colorado
Abstract: One phase of recreation of increasing importance is tourism or travel. An increasing percentage of the consumer dollar is going into travel; and new and expanding business opportunities exist for those who serve the traveling public. To increase the success of these operations, more and better information is needed about the tourist markets; and especially needed are techniques to analyze these potential markets. Here is a brief description of a new technique that can be so used.

Title: Realism in Pricing Analyses
Abstract: Many business firms use formulas based on fully allocated unit cost to determine the selling prices for their products. But is it wise to rely on costs alone? What is the proper role of costs in pricing decisions? By use of an example of a toy manufacturer and of a company producing abrasive grains, at least two significant generalizations are developed.

Title: One Common Market or Six Markets?
Abstract: The U. S. advertiser in the Common-Market countries must beam his message through an unfamiliar and complex media structure in each of them. Even such familiar media as newspapers can fill widely divergent communication roles in the various countries. Here a publisher of media directories in several of the Common-Market countries discusses in broad outline the role, flavor, and kinds of media available to the American marketer.

Title: The Maturing TV Industry
Affiliations: Department of Business Management at Merrimack College, North Andover, Massachusetts
Abstract: Television has now achieved over 90% saturation of electrically wired homes in the United States. Here is a brief summary of the various competitive methods of TV-set manufacturers as to product, price, channels of distribution, and merchandising and advertising.

Title: The Marketing Concept and the Aerospace Business
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration of the University of Southern California, Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago.
Abstract: This article has two purposes. The first is to put the marketing concept into a sociological context, and thus to show that the concept is essential to a theory of the firm. The second purpose is to explain to aerospace firms and their governmental customers why a vigorous marketing organization strengthens the ability of such firms.

Title: The Salesman's Role Revisited
Affiliations: New York State School of Industrial and Labor Relations at Cornell University, Cornell University and Hofstra University.
Abstract: Selection of salesmen, based on the simple concepts of personnel psychology, is one of the most difficult problems for marketing executives. The author of this article holds that selection problems may be traced to a unidimensional view of both the sales jobs and the people who fill them. Instead of this myopic view, he proposes a new view of the salesman's role, involving both interactional and emotional aspects.

Affiliations: Amos Tuck School of Business Administration, Dartmouth College
Abstract: Is the “Truth-in-Packaging Bill” dead or not? More precisely, what about Senator Philip A. Hart's “Fair Packaging and Labeling Act” (S.985)? Here are some answers— and also some provocative thoughts about the obligations of marketing men.

Abstract: Here is an answer to the need for a compensation plan closely tailored to management objectives, and to the abilities and needs of the individual salesman.

Title: Is it Time to Discard the Audience Concept?
Affiliations: Vice President of Marketing Planning and Research of the Bureau of Advertising of the American Newspaper Publishers Association.
Abstract: Marketers often take the term “audience” for granted in evaluating advertising campaigns. But Dr. Leo Bogart presents a case against such uncritical use, arguing that the term has been applied to quite different kinds of measurement, some of dubious validity.

Title: The Influence of Media Characteristics on Coupon Redemption
Affiliations: Director of Market Research of The Reuben H. Donnelley Corporation's Marketing Division, Mt. Vernon, New York.
Abstract: Direct mail, magazine, or newspaper? Are redemption percentages an adequate criterion? Do redemptions “peak” when they appear to? Can residual advertising values be weighed? An analysis of 81 couponing promotions leads to some unexpected conclusions.

Title: A Vast New Storehouse of Transportation and Marketing Data
Affiliations: Vice President, Wilbur Smith and Associates, Inc., California. California Institute of Technology, Yale University Bureau of Highway Traffic.
Abstract: The monumental traffic jam on U. S. streets and highways has sparked a massive program of research in land use, economic data, and travel habits. Current inventories and projections into the future are being organized and recorded in 225 cities across the nation at a cost of about $100 million. This vast new storehouse of data, with immediate application to marketing, is free for the asking, too.

Title: Future Octane Number Requirements for Future Market Demand
Authors: Robert D. Entenberg, Albert L. Menard
Affiliations: Division of Research of the College of Business Administration at the University of Denver; Sonneborn Chemical and Refining Company, New York; Refinery Process Division of Gulf Research and Development Company, Pittsburgh
Abstract: The projection of future octane number requirements for future market demand directly involves a firm's share of the market and its long-run profitability. Octane projections must reflect the probable impact of rapid technological and economic change, as well as ever-changing consumer wants and attitudes. Here is a forecast methodology— an evaluation of the projection of future octane number requirements for marketing strategy.

Title: Alpha Kappa Psi Foundation Award for 1965
Jesting Propensities to Shop
Affiliations: Assistant Professor of Business Administration at the University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Is the consumer a rational being who shops as long as he finds the value of the information so secured to be greater than its cost? A good deal of the literature in marketing might indicate that this is so. But this hypothesis has never been subjected to extensive empirical test. This is why this report on a research project dealing with shopping behavior is of considerable interest.

Title: Testing Propensities to Shop
Time Lag in New Product Development
Affiliations: Vice President for Research and Planning at Pritchard, Wood Incorporated, New York, Director of Marketing Research, Market Planning Department, The Interpublic Group of Companies, Inc.
Abstract: Here is an analysis of 42 case histories, showing that product development is considerably more time-consuming than many marketers realize. The question is—how can time allocations be made more realistic?

Title: Marketing in Italy Today
Affiliations: Professor of Business Administration at Boston University.
Abstract: Italy embodies all stages of economic development in its marketing structure and operations, ranging from regional differences hoary with age … to regulations of distribution based upon the guild system of the Middle Ages … to huge, quasi - independent, state -owned enterprises unusual for a non-Communist state. Here is the most concise and accurate report yet written on marketing in Italy, yesterday and today.

Title: Psychologists in Marketing Education
Affiliations: School of Business Administration at the University of Oregon
Abstract: While the influence of psychology on marketing practices is widely recognized, almost no information is available regarding the roles of psychologists in the education of those preparing for careers in marketing. What related changes are occurring in psychology and in business administration? Are adequate provisions being made so that marketing managers of the future will not have to be self-taught as to their psychological knowledge? Are a sufficient number of psychologists being attracted to the faculties of business schools? This article by a psychologist on the faculty of a school of business provides some answers.

Title: Is Marketing Education Drifting?
Affiliations: Professor of Marketing and Head of the Department of Marketing at The Pennsylvania State University.
Abstract: As marketing becomes more scientific in its orientation and methodology, are the collegiate schools of business responding with more rigorous programs or merely drifting along? Here is the available evidence, and indications of the need for new studies of marketing education.

Title: World Marketing as a New Force for Peace
Abstract: Something new is going on in the world today. Rather than world trade being dependent on world peace, as in times past, world peace may be influenced and brought nearer reality through burgeoning world trade. The author, President of The Coca-Cola Company, has developed this theme in several recent speeches. Here he has condensed his remarks into the present article. He makes a good case to show that trade is crossing borders still closed to diplomats—making greater progress for peace than official conferences.

Title: Behavioral Models for Analyzing Buyers
Affiliations: Associate Professor of Marketing in the School of Business, Northwestern University.
Abstract: What happens in the buyer's mind between the acts of receiving impressions about products and making his purchasing decisions? Several theories exist, but there is no generally accepted comprehensive theory. Here the author contrasts buyer behavioral models based on five major theories, and shows how each has unique marketing applications.

Title: Opportunities and Responsibilities of the Franchised Automobile Dealer
Affiliations: Professor of Marketing and Acting Director of the Program in International Business at the Graduate School of Business Administration of The University of Michigan.
Abstract: This is a sophisticated discussion of the significant changes that have taken place in the automobile industry during the past few years, and the ones that are probably about to take place. If franchised dealers plan well with respect to the changes likely to come, they will have unusual opportunities for successful operation, as this article shows.

Title: Tribute to past Presidents of American Marketing Association
Abstract: This is the speech given by Donald M. Hobart, formerly Senior Vice President and Director of Research of the Curtis Publishing Company (also President of the American Marketing Association in 1945), in New York on June 14, 1965, at the annual meeting of the American Marketing Association.

Title: Marketing Intelligence for Top Management
Affiliations: Wharton School of Finance and Commerce, University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: A number of large companies already have marketing intelligence departments, and others are planning to activate them. What lies behind this recent development in marketing management? What is meant by “marketing intelligence”? How does a company organize for it, and what benefits may be derived from it? Here is the rationale behind this new staff function of business.

Title: Applying an Advertising-Sales Relationship Model to Product Fields
Abstract: The amount spent on advertising a brand, its “momentum” in the product field, and the effectiveness of its advertising are three important factors that can now be measured. Can their relative influence on sales-share change be measured? The President of Schwerin Research reports how this has been done in a broad mathematical model. He believes that the knowledge thus gained will have increasing importance in making realistic decisions in specific brand situations.

Title: The Impact of Retail Coupons
Affiliations: President of the A. C. Nielsen Company, marketing research firm. A graduate of the University of Wisconsin
Abstract: Retail coupons, those small cards or slips of paper that offer the supermarket shopper a few cents off on this product or that, have come of age. They are no longer a nickel-and-dime business. Billions of them are distributed each year by grocery-product manufacturers. Millions of dollars’ worth are redeemed, too, sometimes with tremendous impact on a manufacturer's marketing program. Here are some interesting data about coupons and what makes them so attractive to the contemporary, value-conscious shopper.

Title: The Low Prestige of Personal Selling
Affiliations: Assistant Dean and Associate Professor of Marketing at The University of Toledo.
Abstract: The low social standing of persona I selling is acutely familiar to salesmen, sales managers, and marketing teachers. But the solution to the problem has been an elusive one. Here is a way of placing the problem in its proper perspective, and of removing some of the myths about selling.

Title: A Managerial Approach to Advertising Measurement
Affiliations: Arizona State University as a member of the Department of Marketing
Abstract: This article is based on the findings of a continuing study of advertising measurement that the author is conducting under the auspices of the Planning and Evaluation Committee of the Association of National Advertisers. Since the time that the study started in 1963, data on advertising measurements have been secured from 1,225 individuals in 414 firms in the United States and Canada, and case-history data have been gathered from 50 of these companies. The completed study, to be published in book form, will give case histories of the attempts of national advertisers to measure advertising results — with annual advertising expenditures ranging from under $500,000 to over $50,000,000. One or more case histories from each of the following categories will be included: (1) industrial goods and services, (2) consumer durable goods, (3) consumer nondurable goods, (4) consumer services.

Title: Theodore N. Beckman
Abstract: In these days of mobile professors with shortterm institutional loyalties, a career of 45 years on one faculty is truly remarkable. Such is the record of Theodore N. Beckman, who served The Ohio State University from the time she conferred the Bachelor's degree upon him in 1920 until this June. This long tenure, however, is not the point of the story. It is the variety and scope of Professor Beckman's activities that set him apart. Four labels are needed to describe the man: teacher, author, consultant to government and business, and contributor to marketing thought-all roles performed according to high personal standards of perfection.

Title: Urgently Needed: A Standard Geographic Unit
Affiliations: Director of Marketing Research Oscar Mayer & Company Madison, Wisconsin
Abstract: The first element-number of product or service units sold-usually is defined according to the firm's individual needs. The unit may be sales dollars, cases of cake mix, barrels of beer, hundredweights of meat products, passenger miles traveled, or insurance applications accepted. But there is seldom any doubt about the meaning of the measurement unit or its stability; and yet there is little need for a unit common to all business firms.

Title: Facing up to the “Numbers Business”
Authors: Richard C. Christian, Thomas E. Ryan
Affiliations: Marsteller Inc., Chicago; Inc. New York City

Title: Can Industrial Product Publicity be Measured?
Affiliations: Manager of Marketing Services for Milton Roy Company, St. Petersburg, Florida; Director of Public Relations for the Harry P. Bridge Company, Philadelphia
Abstract: There is no letup in attempts to measure the effectiveness of advertising. But what about attempts to measure the effects of industrial product publicity? The authors of this article assess this important question, and describe an approach to publicity measurement which offers quantitative data for comparison purposes.

Title: “Is Marketing a Science?” Revisited
Affiliations: Dean of the College of Business at Brigham Young University.
Abstract: The term “marketing concept” probably stimulates more interest today than “marketing principles.” Does this less definitive approach impair the hopes of those who aspire to have marketing accepted as a science? Or is it conceivable that the term “science” itself should be viewed in a new perspective? This article favors the latter thesis. And this view should encourage marketing men to employ more scientific resources in quest of more effective marketing management.

Title: Marketing in Nigeria
Affiliations: President of Overseas Economic Development Incorporated of New York, New York
Abstract: Tropical Africa is unlike any other part of the world, and the problems of understanding the commercial systems of the area can be frustrating. Various physical, economic, and social factors lead to marketing procedures that can be radically unusual. This author analyzes and describes the marketing patterns and techniques found in Nigeria, and outlines some of the changes that are taking place as the country develops.

Title: The Woman's Day Case and Cooperative Advertising
Affiliations: Associate Professor of Business Administration at the University of Kentucky.
Abstract: Section 2(d) of the Robinson-Patman Act seeks to regulate cooperative advertising. The “Woman's Day” case raises some important questions concerning the type of marketing activities to be regulated under Section 2(d). One such question is: What is cooperative advertising?

Title: Patterns of Communication in Marketing Organizations
Authors: R. Clifton Andersen, Edward W. Cundiff
Affiliations: Associate Professor of Marketing Administration at the University of Texas
Abstract: The authors of this article conducted extensive interviews in four large consumer goods firms, to study horizontal communication patterns among executives with marketing responsibilities. Their study gives factual information, especially about the “informal communication network” in such organizations.

Title: A Marketing Model for Short-term Prediction of Consumer Sales
Affiliations: Lawrence College, Northwestern University, the Harvard Graduate School of Business Administration, and the Columbia University School of General Studies.
Abstract: This article is a nontechnical description of a generalized marketing model from the point of view of the manufacturer of nondurable goods, one who does not fully control his own distribution system. The model seeks to identify the main marketing variables affecting the sales of such products. These are arranged in a structure which offers a useful conceptual approach for marketing management, and a starting framework for a specific information-system design. Mr. Barton believes that it is technically feasible to collect input statistics with sufficient accuracy as to improve the marketing activities of many medium-size to large-size companies.

Title: Modern Methods for Local Delivery Route Design
Abstract: Improving the design of routes and thereby reducing delivery costs is a major marketing problem. Here is a practical case study in which hundreds of trucks and thousands of customers were involved, and with interesting results.

Title: Have Manufacturing Firms Adopted the Marketing Concept?
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration, Elizabethtown College.

Title: Blueprint for Marketing
Abstract: Famed Commander Whitehead's views about marketing are “capsuled” in this brief article. The material has been adapted from a portion of one of a series of articles by Commander Whitehead appearing in the British publication MARKETING, produced by the Institute of Marketing and Sales Management.

Title: The Marketing Dilemma of Negroes
Authors: Raymond A. Bauer, Scott M. Cunningham, Lawrence H. Wortzel
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration, Harvard University.
Abstract: The behavior of Negroes in the marketplace is shown to be integrally related to attempts to find full status in American Society. According to the authors, the Negro market divides “spontaneously” into two segments on the extent to which individual Negroes make the efforts to achieve this full status.

Title: How Can the Advertising Dollar Work Harder?
How Much Does an Industrial Logotype Add to the Effectiveness of an Advertisement?
How Much Does an Industrial Logotype Add to the Effectiveness of an Advertisement?
Riesman Revisited
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration at the University of California, Los Angeles.
Abstract: Marketing practitioners and authors of textbooks on marketing are paying increasing attention to behavioral science materials, such as Riesman's conceptualizations of social character. This article is a brief presentation of the Riesman thesis, and of the misinterpretations of that thesis made by some people in marketing.

Title: The Carry-over Effect of Advertising
Abstract: Most advertisers believe there is a carry-over effect of advertising. What evidence is available, and what does it indicate about the relationships of sales to advertising? The author of this article presents a case study, and examines other evidence bearing on this question. He also constructs models involving repeat purchasing and impression cumulation as underlying reasons for a carry-over effect.

Title: Two Requirements for Measuring the Effectiveness of Promotion
Affiliations: Research Division Manager in the Market Research and Planning Department of The Atlantic Refining Company.
Abstract: Is it really true that so many factors influence sales that it is impossible to identify and measure the contribution of individual factors? Not so, says this author, who holds that there are procedures available for producing meaningful measurements of promotion.

Title: Increasing the Power of Research to Guide Advertising Decisions
Affiliations: Survey Research Unit of the London School of Economics
Abstract: Mass media research must provide decision makers with the most relevant information available, and must provide it accurately. It does not always do so. This article features the intensive interview, extended piloting and the intensive backtracking interview as techniques for assessing the relevance and the accuracy of media, measures currently in use and for developing more efficient alternatives where this is necessary.

Title: Further Pursuit of the Dissonant Consumer: A Comment
Abstract: A clarification is offered by a marketing man as to the pursuit of the dissonant consumer.

Title: Sales Variability in Service Stations
Abstract: The fact that individual retail outlets differ substantially from one another in sales volume is not news to marketing executives. Yet static patterns for measuring retail success and failure continue in use. The author of this article demonstrates the extent of retail sales variations in the oil industry. He also shows evidence that the use of fixed sales ratios may lead to inaccuracies in appraisals of stations and managers, and to inefficient allocation of marketing expenditures.

Title: Dilemma of Selling to Uncle Sam
Abstract: More than $50 billion are spent annually by the United States Government for defense purposes. The author of this article takes a brief look at vital factors influencing a decision of whether or not an industrial firm should attempt to find a niche in the Government procurement system.

Title: Is Marketing Education Driving or Drifting?
Abstract: “Because of its fundamental and continuing interest in marketing education, the Marketing Science Institute has completed a factual study of trends in marketing course offerings and enrollments in the member schools of the American Association of Collegiate Schools of Business. “Although the accompanying background study raises many questions, it does provide a foundation for identification and discussion of some major issues. The full report of the findings of MSI's study is available from the Marketing Science Institute, 3625 Walnut Street, Philadelphia 4, Pennsylvania.” (Wendell R. Smith, Pres., Marketing Science Institute)

Title: The Marketing Manager's Dilemma
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Columbia University.
Abstract: To research or not to research. That is a question that often plagues the marketing manager. Should he spend money on marketing research to get more facts so that a given operating decision may be sounder? Or should he save the money and make the decision without the added information a research would supply, thereby accepting an increased risk of decision error? Professor Alexander suggests a systematic approach to the twin problems of deciding when marketing research is worth while, and of making it a more useful tool in the kit of the marketing manager.

Title: Trading Stamps in Japan—Boom in the Making?
Authors: A. J. Alton, George O. Totten
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Advertising, University of Rhode Island; Eastern Michigan University
Abstract: As excitement concerning trading stamps diminishes in the United States, and controversy abounds in Great Britain's venture, a stamp boom is taking place in Japan. The rapid development of trading stamps in Japan is analyzed in this article by a marketing specialist who has been a student of the trading-stamp industry in the United States for a number of years, and by a specialist in Japanese political and economic life.

Title: How International Can European Advertising Be?
Affiliations: Board of the Swedish Sales Institute, Stockholm.
Abstract: Is it true that the various markets in Europe are so different that the same message for the same product cannot appeal as successfully to two or three or more markets as a campaign tailormade for a single nation? Here is how an internationally-recognized advertising man answers this question.

Title: Passport for Marketing Overseas
Abstract: Ray Eppert, a recognized expert in the field of international marketing, contends that it is mandatory for U.S. marketing management to become internationally minded at all levels, or else face complete failure even at home. Originally titled “Passport for World Leadership,” the basic precepts in this article come from the Charles Coolidge Parlin Memorial Lecture given by Mr. Eppert at the American Marketing Association meeting in Philadelphia in May, 1964.

Title: Effective Management and the Human Factor
Affiliations: Chicago, New York, Los Angeles, Toronto, and London
Abstract: Management executives—especially in marketing—are striving to become more scientific. Disciplines for evaluating, measuring, and predicting are the current growth fields of business. But are these disciplines carrying management further away from where the problems really are? The ideas expressed in this article run somewhat counter to the schools of thought so dominant in today's front offices and some schools of business—and some different answers are suggested.

Industrial Marketing: Physical Distribution: Key to Improved Volume and Profits
Authors: Richard C. Christian, Wendell M. Stewart

Title: Physical Distribution: Key to Improved Volume and Profits
Abstract: D is the sale and movement of goods to customers. term physical refers to that portion of the total distribution activity devoted to the addition of time and place utility to the form utility provided by manufacturing. Physical distribution has been variously described as The Economy's Dark Continent,^ and the last frontier of cost reduction in American business. You can't cut prices, labor or material. only fat left in this business is (physical) distribution.2 These typical comments highlight a condition which is receiving greatly increased management attention in today's highly competitive industrial marketing economy: the fact' that improvements in distribution technology have not kept pace with improvements in manufacturing efficiency and marketing effectiveness. WENDELL M. STEWART

Title: Alpha Kappa Psi Foundation Award for 1964
Concepts in Comparative Retailing
Abstract: An increasing volume of descriptive material about marketing in various nations has become available in recent years; few attempts have been made to generalize about all nations. This article, focusing on one aspect of this broad problem, presents a framework for generalizing about retail operating methods in different marketing systems.

Title: Wanted: Sates Managers for Marketing Research
Abstract: Despite significant improvements in methodology, many corporate executives are skeptical about the profit contribution being made by marketing research. Does management fail to appreciate the true value of research? Or have some research practitioners neglected a key part of their responsibilities? This article identifies a gap between marketing research practice and its profitable application to day-today business problems. The author goes on to suggest an approach for narrowing the gap.

Title: Wanted: Sales Managers for Marketing Research
The Wide C-Post and the Fashion Process
Abstract: Fashions are self-fulfilling prophecies, and arise through a process of agreement among fashion-makers responding to common situational cues. Consumer behavior is only one of these cues. This view of the fashion process is illustrated by the wide C-post, which has become a dominant fashion in automobile styling during the past ten years.

Title: Marketing Technology, Tasks, and Relationships
Abstract: What is the place of traditional marketing analysis in recent managerial, social, and quantitative interpretations of marketing? Here is a framework for the integration of marketing thought in the concept of marketing as a social process.

Title: A Statement of Marketing Philosophy
Abstract: This statement is a summary of the basic ideas or convictions about marketing which are shared by the marketing faculty of The Ohio State University. It was formulated by them in order to provide the faculty with a formally stated sense of purpose … a means of unifying individual efforts … a tool for achieving consistency … a guideline for maintaining charted courses … a basis for evaluating marketing educational and research programs … a prerequisite to the development of a formally stated philosophy of marketing education … and a statement to clarify their views to the academic and business community.

Title: Is the Cost Defense Workable?
Abstract: The cost defense under the Robinson-Patman Act once seemed to be a fairly routine process. Since 1962, however, serious problems have been posed by the Supreme Court and the Federal Trade Commission. This article examines the cost defense in the light of these decisions.

Title: Planning and Executing an Effective Agricultural Promotion Program
Affiliations: U. S. Army Natick Laboratories, Natick, Massachusetts
Abstract: More than 1,100 organized commodity groups in-invest over $75 million each year for advertising and promotional purposes. This article reviews some current thinking on agricultural promotion programs. The principles stated at the end of the article may be applicable to product promotion both within and without the area of agriculture.

Title: Marketing in the Industrialization of Underdeveloped Countries
Affiliations: National Institute of Management Development, Cairo, U.A.R.
Abstract: Industrialization has lured many underdeveloped countries as the fastest and surest method of economic development. But marketing problems are causing unexpected difficulties in many of these countries—difficulties that were not anticipated because production has been seen as almost the only problem. This article demonstrates the pivotal role of marketing.

Title: What is the Next Breakthrough in Research?
Abstract: Many of the tools that marketing researchers have can help to overcome selling obstacles. But what does it matter how precise their techniques are if researchers cannot persuade managements how and when to use these techniques? Nothing happens until somebody sells something. This applies to marketing research, too.

Title: Product Characteristics and Marketing Strategy
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration, The University of Michigan
Abstract: There is real need for increasingly rigorous generalizations and analytical models of the behavior of the elements in any given marketing system. The model presented here provides a means of predicting, or justifying, a marketing mix for a product with given characteristics.

Title: A Shift in the Point-of-Purchase?
Affiliations: Dean L. Burdick Associates, Inc., a New York advertising-marketing agency
Abstract: The prospective customer who feels the necessity of making his own personal evaluation of merchandise usually makes the retail establishment his point-of purchase. However, as the customer increases his willingness to rely on others for shopping information and guidance, his point-of-purchase can shift away from the store and into the home or office. The author shows why this is happening and he gives some interesting implications. Other factors contributing to such a shift, and the implications of the growth of this away-from-the-store shopping are also discussed.

Title: Behavioral Science Offers Fresh Insights on New Product Acceptance
Affiliations: Bureau of Business and Economic Research in the School of Business Administration, University of South Carolina
Abstract: In spite of enormous sums of money spent for research and development, an estimated 90% of all new products fail within four years of their introduction. The explanation, says the author, is not that consumer behavior is fickle and unpredictable, but rather that marketing managers do not fully understand the processes by which consumers accept or reject an innovation. In this article he indicates what the contributions of the behavioral sciences might be.

Title: Are you Really Planning your Marketing?
Affiliations: Headquarters Planning Department of Mobil Oil Company, in New York
Abstract: What is wrong with the marketing planning methods many companies use? Can something useful be learned by examining the procedures of leading companies and reviewing the literature of planning? What should a company do NOW to improve its marketing planning?

Title: Dynamics of New Product Campaigns
Affiliations: Federal Systems Division, IBM.; Iowa State, Princeton, and New York Universities.
Abstract: Introducing a new consumer product on a nationwide basis is much like playing a game of stud poker. Consumer reactions early in the campaign, when sufficiently well understood, can provide vital clues in accelerating or cutting off product promotion as required for maximum impact to corporate objectives.

Title: Critical Path Analysis for New Product Planning
Affiliations: A.B. in Physics from Princeton University; New York University; Univac Division of Sperry Rand Corporation in New York City
Abstract: Since its inception in 1957, Critical Path Analysis (CPA), which includes the CRITICAL PATH METHOD (CPM), and PROGRAM EVALUATION AND REVIEW TECHNIQUE (PERT) has received widespread acclaim as a planning, scheduling, and control tool. Its applications had been initially restricted to construction and engineering. Growing sophistication in the use of the tool has extended its applicability to the area of new product planning. The purpose of this article is to introduce to marketing managers and analysts the group of techniques called CPA and its application to new product planning. The process of new product planning as a function of marketing management is first described. The concept and the underlying logic of CPA and a hypothetical new product venture are presented to show the technique's rationale and capability. Extensions of CPA and its value in a new product venture conclude the discussion.

Title: EQ, Son of EQ, and the Reaction Profile
Affiliations: Rutgers University, and Head of the Developmental Research Unit at Benton & Bowles, Inc.
Abstract: Are consumers' ratings of advertisements definitive enough to yield valid information about effectiveness? Or do such ratings register consumers' likes and dislikes, and nothing more? The author conducted a series of experiments on advertisement rating scales. He concludes that consumers' ratings can order advertisements along at least two, and perhaps three, different and important dimensions. He further indicates that results obtained from rating scales have a useful relationship to the results obtained from another well-known advertising-testing method, that of aided recall.

Title: Reducing Advertising Failures by Concept Testing
Abstract: How can concept testing be used to reduce the risk of advertising failures? For which specific purposes is concept testing well-suited; for which is it ill-suited? The author examines the logic of four specific rationales and techniques, and provides some interesting answers.

Title: Designing Marketing Research to Increase Validity
Affiliations: Leo Burnett Company, Inc.; Chemical engineering from Iowa State College; University of Chicago.
Abstract: How valid are the results of marketing research that involve people as the subjects? Is it possible to waste large sums of money because of reliance on research systems that have built-in errors, or that show results not applicable to the untested population at large? Since all marketing data are based in one way or another on actions of people, and since people and groups of people are so varied, careful attention to the design of marketing research experiments is sorely needed. In his forthcoming book, EXPERIMENTATION IN MARKETING (New York: McGraw-Hill), the author devotes his second chapter to experimental research designs involving people or groups of people. This article is a condensation of that chapter.

Title: Probabilistic Models of Consumer Buying Behavior
Authors: Alfred A. Kuehn, Ralph L. Day
Affiliations: Graduate School of Industrial Administration, Carnegie Institute of Technology, and founder of Market Science Associates, Inc.; Pennsylvania State University, and University of Texas and Carnegie Institute of Technology.; Georgia Institute of Technology; University of North Carolina.
Abstract: Does it make sense to classify consumers as users and nonusers? As heavy and light users? As users of brand X rather than brand Y? Do American consumers fit into such neat categories? Or is it likely that their brand choice behavior is more subtle, less susceptible to exact categorization? This article shows how traditional, static approaches are inadequate for predicting consumer behavior. It offers an alternative: the dynamic, probabilistic approach which can sharpen analysis and yield better predictive models.

Title: Limitations of Supermarkets in Spain
Affiliations: St. Joseph's College, Philadelphia, and University of Dayton and at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.
Abstract: Will successful marketing institutions in economically advanced nations succeed when introduced into less developed economies? A study of Spain's recent experience with supermarkets reveals some of the roadblocks that hold back the adoption of new marketing institutions.

Title: Marketing in Spain
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration at the University of Minnesota.; University of Pennsylvania.
Abstract: The Spain of modern times has been an ultra-conservative nation in virtually every respect: economic, political, religious, and social. But Spain has attained some measure of financial and economic stability within the last five years, and now stands on the threshold of a new economic era. An efficient marketing structure will be a necessary concomitant of any real economic advancement. The author surveys the current state of marketing in Spain, and indicates some of the steps that will be required for the improvement of the Spanish marketing system.

Title: The Pluses and Minuses of Branding Agricultural Products
Affiliations: Marketing at Michigan Technological University.; Colorado State University
Abstract: Differentiation of homogeneous agricultural products through branding is a difficult and costly undertaking for a firm. How successful has this been, and what are the possibilities for additional brand promotion? As a specific example, the author shows the effects of brands upon consumer preferences for frozen, whole turkey.

Title: Latest Developments in Automatic Retailing in Europe
Affiliations: London School of Economics and the University of Genoa.
Abstract: Will automatic selling grow to dominate certain fields of retailing? For many years European retailers have set up coin-operated machines in front of their stores, offering goods after closing hours and on holidays. Recently some have been experimenting with completely automatic retailing. This article describes the latest developments in this growing trend, stressing the important role played by technical, marketing, and psychological factors.

Title: How Advertising Became Respectable
Abstract: Dr. Charles K. Ramond suggests that sooner or later most companies will measure the return on their advertising as readily as they do the return on their other capital investments. And he also predicts that knowledge of the profitability of advertising will gradually inhibit tasteless advertising, thereby muting the public criticism some advertising men feel so keenly. Here is a “history” of the next 35 years of U.S. advertising.

Legal developments in marketing
