More detailed information about individual items may be obtained by reference to the source cited for each case. References to CCH are to the Commerce Clearing House Trade Regulation Reporter; references to BNA are to Bureau of National Affairs, Antitrust & Trade Regulation Report.

Title: Legal Developments in Marketing
Frank Stanton
How Stable Are Advertiser-Advertising Agency Relationships?
Affiliations: Director of Market Planning Oscar Mayer & Company Madison, Wisconsin
Abstract: W HEN a large advertiser decides to switch advertising agencies, it is usually front-page news in the advertising press. And since there is often a faithful reporting of account changes even among relatively small advertisers, most issues of these business papers contribute to a general impression that client-agency relations lack stability. The following analysis was made in order to answer three questions: 1. Among large companies, how stable are clientagency relationships ? 2. How does this stability (or lack of it) vary by company type? 3. How do sales and earnings of companies that switch agencies compare with those of companies that stay with the same agency? The Fortune list of 500 largest U. S. industrial corporations provided a convenient list of large companies.' These companies accounted for more than half the 1962 sales of all U. S. manufacturing and mining companies, and for more than 70% of their profits. The smallest corporation on the list had sales of $83 millions. The 1952 edition of the Standard Advertising Register was consulted in order to determine the major agency employed by each company in that year.2 The Standard Advertising Register for 1963 was used to determine the major agency of each

Title: Growth Perspective for Industrial Advertising
Affiliations: Marsteller Inc., Chicago; Manager, Advertising & Sales Promotion Worthington Corporation Harrison, New Jersey

Title: The Use of Transportation Data in Market Pattern Analysis
Affiliations: The Ronald Press Company in 1958 and of several monographs and articles on transportation and related subjects
Abstract: Most marketing data on consumption and production are out of date before they are available or do not lend themselves to easy analysis. This article describes an easily understood technique for the analysis of market patterns, which uses reliable, timely, and available data to link specific production centers to specific consumption centers.

Title: Management Responsibilities Facing the Wholesale Grocer
Affiliations: Lecturer on Food Distribution and Comparative Marketing at the Harvard Business School
Abstract: The world of the grocery wholesaler has changed and is continuing to change dramatically. What are the objectives of the marketer in this area? What are his responsibilities and how should he meet them? In discussing these questions as they apply to the food - distribution industry, the author hits upon background, objectives, and responsibilities that apply to other areas of business enterprise as well. He also constructs a “model” grocery wholesaler whose behavior reflects how management could face its responsibilities.

Title: The Pursuit of the Dissonant Consumer
Affiliations: Sociology and Social Psychology at the University of Chicago.
Abstract: Do you fully understand the latest fad in consumer research—the study of DISSONANT consumers? The author of this thought-provoking article explains the complications and pitfalls of research in this area.

Title: Credit Management as a Marketing Function
Abstract: The supposed antithesis of credit and marketing management has hindered the development and integration of both. Through the application of newer concepts of management to credit management, the author believes that ways are open for achievement of broader marketing objectives.

Title: Wholesaling in an Economy of Scarcity: Turkey
Abstract: This article analyzes the functions of wholesaling in an economy of SCARCITY, the Turkish economy, in contrast to the functions of wholesaling in an economy of ABUNDANCE, the United States. The author compares the two systems, based on firsthand knowledge.

Title: Uses of Sociology in Studying “Consumption” Behavior
Authors: Charles Y. Glock, Francesco M. Nicosia
Affiliations: Survey Research Center at the University of California at Berkeley; School of Business Administration at the University of California at Berkeley, and Director of the Consumer Behavior Program
Abstract: Although there has been a growth in the amount of social science dealing with consumers, for the most part sociologists have not been concerned with the study of the AGGREGATE behavior of consumers. Here is a discussion of some of the ways that sociological theories and methods may contribute toward the prediction and explanation of aggregate consumption behavior.

Title: Simulation for Decision Making in Marketing
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration at the University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: Simulation is an approach to problem solving which has as its focus the construction and study of computer models as descriptions of the problem being analyzed. Its usefulness in marketing comes from the fact that problems too complicated for analysis by conventional methods may be solved. The author gives several examples of how this is coming true.

Title: Assumptions in Measuring Advertising Effectiveness
Abstract: Thomas E. Coffin's article, “A Pioneering Experiment in Assessing Advertising Effectiveness,” published in the July, 1963, issue outlined a logical model and a practical research approach, and indicated further improvements to be made. However, the author of the present article believes that certain basic assumptions need further study.

Title: A Realistic Division of Downtown Retailing
Abstract: Is the presently designated central business district retailing area of cities too narrowly defined? Yes, says the author of this article. He advances the concepts of the central business district “core” and “frame.” His analysis of downtown retailing might lead to more realistic divisions of downtown versus suburban retailing facilities.

Title: Defining and Estimating a Trading Area
Abstract: What are the conceptual properties of a trading area? What is the definition of the term? What testable propositions are currently available to validate its properties and thus give precision to the definition? This article gives answers to these questions.

Title: Introducing the Marketing Channel to Price Theory
Affiliations: Senior Consultant of Marketing and Economics for P. S. Ross & Partners, Management Consultants, Canada.
Abstract: Economic price theory has much to contribute to organized marketing thought. Likewise the reality of microeconomic price theory can be improved by its incorporation of marketing concepts. The author reviews several price theories, which if properly integrated, could aid marketing theory as applied to the important area of marketing channels.

Title: A New Theory of Consumer Buying Intent
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Distribution at Clarkson College of Technology, Potsdam, New York.
Abstract: Do products have certain characteristics which establish the relative importance of basic elements of the marketing mix? Here is an attempt to provide a framework by which all products may be related for conceptual and practical purposes. Rather than classify products, the unusual approach developed in this article involves the establishment of a spectrum as a model. All products can be located on this spectrum of consumer buying intent by the measurement of product characteristics.

Title: Who Does the Work of Retailing?
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, is Professor of Marketing at Michigan State University.
Abstract: Many activities of retailers can be divided among manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, specialized functionaries, and consumers in many different ways. But which marketing tasks should retailers perform, share, shift, and contract out? Here are some thought-provoking answers by a specialist on retailing.

Title: Intensive Competitive Marketing
Affiliations: Young and Rubicam Inc., New York.
Abstract: The author shows how selective planning can be accomplished effectively through the INTENSIVE COMPETITIVE MARKETING AUDIT—a technique which calls for study of the total marketing activities of a company and its major competitors at each level of distribution. A basic check list is included. Answers to the questions asked should result in the pinpointing of profit opportunities in specific markets through the identification of competitive vulnerability.

Title: A New Method for Testing Pricing Decisions
Affiliations: Vice President of Market Facts, Inc., Chicago.
Abstract: All business executives agree that pricing decisions are important. But far too many do not fully associate THE pricing decision and absolute dollar profitability. Here is a description of a special technique for measuring relationships between alternative prices and demand.

Title: Marketing's Little-Known Microscope
Affiliations: O. E. McIntyre, Inc., New York
Abstract: Vast quantities of marketing information are gathered and tabulated every 10 years in the United States Census, but only a small fraction of these data are used by the average marketer. Detailed to the point of being almost microscopic and supremely useful when properly employed, the census-tract tabulations have not been popularly used in the past. The author explains how census-tract tabulations can be put to work, and gives details on the application of this highly sophisticated tool to several forms of marketing.

Title: Everett R. Smith
Abstract: O MOST marketing executives and teachers Everett R. Smith, Director of Marketing and Research of Macfadden-Bartell Corporation, is a familiar figure as an active member and past president of this association. A Connecticut Yankee and direct descendant of Roger Williams (founder of Rhode Island), Everett R. Smith was born and grew up in New Haven. He received his B.A. cum laude from Yale in 1907 and was a top-ranking member of Phi Beta Kappa. After graduation he started in the newspaper field, soon became city editor, and then moved to the position of business and advertising manager of the New Haven Journal-Courier. Everett Smith's interests soon changed, and he turned to other fields of business. He became a salesman of farm equipment. He joined an advertising agency, but in 1926 became an advertising and sales executive of one of its clients,ERET the Fuller Brush Company. As Advertising Manager of the Fuller Brush Company, he planned their first massive advertising campaign. This effort was notable at that time for its size of operations; and his carefully planned campaigns became major factors which resulted in the rapid development and expansion of Fuller Brush

Title: How Can the Marketing Man Market Himself?
Affiliations: Market Planning Oscar Mayer & Company Madison, Wisconsin

Title: First Things First in Industrial Advertising
Authors: Richard C. Christian, Marshall C. Lewis

Title: Speaking of Consumers
Abstract: This is James O. Peck-ham's reply to John L. Mason's reply (see the preceding pages, 68–69) to Mr. Peckham's article, “The Consumer Speaks.”

Title: A Few Consumers Speak
Affiliations: The University of Toledo, Indiana University, General Electric Company
Abstract: A recent article by James O. Peckham in the JOURNAL OF MARKETING entitled “The Consumer Speaks” was of considerable interest to many readers. With real concern over the possibility that the Peckham article might be given too great acceptance, the author of the present article raises several questions about the conclusions reached.

Title: Why Bother to Decrease Interview Refusals?
Affiliations: Marketing and Sales Research Department of Merck Sharp and Dohme, Division of Merck and Company, Inc.
Abstract: This is a pointed criticism of an article in a recent issue of the JOURNAL OF MARKETING that described a method used in cutting the refusal rate of respondents.

Title: Concentration by Salesmen on Congenial Prospects
Affiliations: Equitable Life Assurance Society, Prudential Insurance Company, Oberlin College and Columbia University
Abstract: Prospects easy to approach and who provide the most pleasant company are not necessarily those most likely to purchase. A method is described here for determining whether salesmen are spending disproportionate effort on the approachable prospects.

Title: Manufacturer's Representative or Company Salesman?
Abstract: There are many situations that make one kind of sales organization preferable to another, but what is the industrial buyer's preference? Does it matter to the industrial buyer whether a salesman is a manufacturer's representative or a direct company man? The results of a survey in the electronic components' industry indicate some possible answers.

Title: Effective Techniques in Industrial Marketing Research
Abstract: Is industrial marketing research really as simple and straightforward as it is made out to be? Is there more to it than just “freewheeling” interviews with a few hand-picked respondents? Why is there so little published about industrial marketing research? Why is methodology so lacking in industrial marketing research? Here are some answers to these questions by a Dutch marketing specialist.

Title: Conditioning Effects from Repeated Household Interviews
Affiliations: School of Business Administration, University of Minnesota, Columbia University, U. S. Bureau of the Census.; Statistical Methods Division, U. S. Bureau of the Census, College of the City of New York, New York University and American University
Abstract: Repeated interviews with the same households are often conducted in surveys. Does this repeated interviewing affect the behavior and reports of the respondents? The answer has important implications for survey design. This article provides some evidence on the effects of repeated interviewing in a household expenditures survey.

Title: Pretesting Field Interviewing Costs through Simulation
Affiliations: The Amos Tuck School of Business Administration at Dartmouth College, The University of Michigan, University of Toronto.
Abstract: Determination of the cost implications of alternate field procedures and sample designs has been a thorny problem for those conducting field surveys. This article shows how computer simulation can provide a fast, accurate, and inexpensive solution to these kinds of problems.

Title: Forecasting Brand Performance through Simulation Experiments
Affiliations: Krannert Graduate School of Industrial Administration of Purdue University.
Abstract: How can marketing managers develop sound alternative marketing strategies and forecast their relative effectiveness? Simulation techniques may be the answer. Although these techniques and the methods of analysis may not be familiar to most marketing men, their potential usefulness is demonstrated in this article.

Title: Let's “Internationalize” Our Marketing Students
Affiliations: Transportation, and International Business at the University of Washington.
Abstract: Every year hundreds of thousands of graduates of American colleges and universities enter business, with almost no knowledge of international business relationships. How can marketing educators help to correct this deficiency? The author of this article has a very practical suggestion, based on the development of a different type of course in basic marketing.

Title: Is Advertising Important in the Soviet Economy?
Affiliations: International Mass Communications at the School of Journalism of the University of Iowa
Abstract: In the Soviet Union's planned society where the means of production and distribution are government and Party monopolies, commercial advertising would appear to be superfluous. Official Soviet policy has always spurned advertising as economic waste and has at times denounced advertising and other “bourgeois capitalistic” devices as competition, production differentiation, and installment buying. Why, then, is commercial advertising “catching on” in the Soviet Union and changing established marketing practices? This article traces and evaluates the rise of this surprising new development in the leading Communist state.

Title: Variations in the Cyclical Behavior of Advertising
Abstract: The general pattern of cyclical fluctuations in advertising has become familiar today. But what remains less well understood is how one type of advertising may behave differently from others. A better insight into this subject will help media in reducing business instability and to assist advertisers in planning effective advertising strategies. This article demonstrates how differently advertisers of different types of products and of various sizes react to business fluctuations.

Title: Retail Competition in Chile
Authors: Rolf J. Luders, Allen F. Jung
Affiliations: Catholic University in Santiago, Chile, University of Chicago.; Graduate School of Business Downtown Program, University of Chicago
Abstract: Although there is a very limited market for durable goods in Chile, there is considerable competition among retail merchants. Variations in price and finance charges are reported in the present study.

Title: Retailing in Poland: A First-Hand Report
Affiliations: The George Washington University, in Washington, D. C., Graduate School of Business and Public Administration of Cornell University; Wharton School of Finance and Commerce of the University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: An extensive exchange of letters between Professor J. Hart Walters, Jr., and various Polish economists resulted in a first-hand study of marketing in Poland for almost one year. Drawing on his first-hand experiences in Poland, as well as documentary sources, the author shows why low costs of doing business in Poland are not always accompanied by a high degree of consumer convenience. As in other Eastern European economies, Polish retailing is relatively decentralized, but many major areas of decision-making are centrally controlled.

Title: The “Imageries” of Department Stores
Authors: Stuart U. Rich, Bernard D. Portis
Affiliations: University of Oregon, Harvard Business School; University of Western Ontario, Harvard Business School, Harvard University
Abstract: What is it that really constitutes a store's “image”? How do downtown department stores and suburban department stores differ in imagery? Here are the highlights of a study of the shopping attitudes of 4,500 women shoppers — the different types of appeal in department stores, the different customer characteristics, differences in shopping behavior, and differences between the imagery of suburban branch department stores and their “parent” stores in the city.

Title: Is a Marketing Man Just a Marketing Man?
Abstract: If “marketing man” is a stilted, undignified, and archaic term for those engaged in marketing work— as the author of this article claims—what can be done about it? How about a new name for marketing practitioners and teachers?

Title: The Death and Burial of “Sick” Products
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Miami University, and Seton Hall University.
Abstract: Products, like men, are mortal. They flourish for a time, then decline and die. While the death of a man is catastrophic in the sense that it occurs at a specific point in time, that of a product tends to be an indefinite process that may continue until its last user forgets that it ever existed and so will no longer try to buy it. Professor R. S. Alexander presents a thoughtful and practical plan for selecting products for elimination; gathering information about them; making decisions about them; and, if necessary, removing the doomed products from the line.

True Correlates of Automobile Shopping Behavior
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, University of Chicago.
Abstract: In the October, 1962, JOURNAL OF MARKETING Franklin B. Evans presented data as to kinds of shopping behavior exhibited by automobile purchasers. The October, 1963, issue contained a three-fold critique by Joseph R. Murphy of the Evans article. Here is the Evans reply to the Murphy reply to the original article by Evans.

Title: The “Older” Market—Fact or Fiction?
Affiliations: Louisiana State University in New Orleans.
Abstract: Does the “over-65” market have real significance for most American firms today? Figures on income and expenditure provide some interesting clues. They are of special interest to marketing executives who are contemplating “senior citizens” as a market target.

Title: The Case for Redefining Services
Affiliations: College of Commerce of DePaul University.
Abstract: Services are a large part of total marketing transactions each year, yet have had little attention in marketing literature. A remedy for this condition is proposed in the form of a redefinition of services and division of all service activities into a threefold grid: Rented Goods Services, Owned Goods Services, and Non-Goods Services.

Title: Marketing the Transit System
Affiliations: University of California at Berkeley in 1957. General Contracting Company, Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia.
Abstract: Passenger transit companies in many cities are now municipally owned, and the trend to municipal ownership has accelerated in the past decade. As a result, city governments are faced with serious marketing problems for the transportation services they are selling. City-owned transit systems have inherited the marketing problems of the earlier private companies. Here is a discussion of how these problems evolved, and the implications for the cities and citizens involved.

Title: Local Media Analysis through Marketing Considerations
Affiliations: Group Media Director in Cunningham & Walsh, New York advertising agency, Media Department at Compton Advertising.
Abstract: Advertisers are constantly confronted with the problem of budget distribution. Although much progress has been made in the measurement of both marketing data and advertising weight, little has been accomplished in terms of correlating the two so as to arrive at a sound basis for budgeting decisions. This article offers a practical approach for the budget planner who wishes to allocate monies to markets on the basis of the markets’ estimated productivity.

Title: How Important is Pricing in Competitive Strategy?
Abstract: Most economic theory relating to business behavior emphasizes pricing. Also, the economist traditionally attempts to explain marketing strategy in terms of monopolistic and competitive market structures. This approach is challenged by the author of this article. According to his research, the product and the customer are the determining factors in a company's marketing strategy.

Title: New Reasoning in Choosing a Warehouse Location
Abstract: Should a company in need of additional warehouse space expand in already crowded quarters or pack up and move to more copious surroundings? Optimum solution of such a problem involves candid appraisal of the present and wise prediction of future needs. That such a decision cannot be made by hunch or crystal ball is apparent. But how should it be made? In this article, the author shows how a Los Angeles distributor assigned values to various warehouse location considerations to work out the expansion problem.

Title: Logical Flow Models for Marketing Analysis
Authors: William F. Massy, Jim D. Savvas
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Stanford University.; Jim D. Savvas and Associates, Bay City, Michigan.
Abstract: Can analytical models of marketing phenomena be constructed, tested, and understood by persons who are not sophisticated in mathematics? “Yes,” say the authors—LOGICAL FLOW MODELS meet the specifications. They are appropriate for the analysis of large classes of marketing behavior. They can yield specific predictions, or be made the basis for computer simulation and sensitivity analysis in much the same manner as their mathematical counterparts. They can be important aids to decision making.

Title: The Retail Hardware Decline
Abstract: Until recently the hardware store held a place of prominence among retail institutions, but it is gradually losing that important position. What has caused the retail hardware trade to experience this decline? What, if anything, can hardware retailers do to rectify this situation? The author examines statistical evidence to ascertain the need for some changes, and gives concrete suggestions as to what directions these changes might lead.

Title: Market Performance in the Baking Industry
Authors: David A. Storey, Paul L. Farris
Affiliations: Department of Agriculture and Food Economics at the University of Massachusetts.; Agricultural Economics at Purdue University.
Abstract: This article sets forth the key market structure characteristics and developments of the perishable bakery products industry. It is concerned with questions of how the industry performs and how patterns of organization and behavior influence performance. The approach here can also be useful in analyzing the market structure and behavior of other industries.

Title: Changes in Retail Trade Flow
Affiliations: Bureau of Business and Economic Research and Professor of Marketing, Michigan State University.
Abstract: Is the plight of downtown retailing wholly attributable to the movement of population and business activity to the suburbs? The author of this article analyzes changes in population and retail-trade concentrations, and concludes that metropolitan retailing (downtown and suburban combined) has become less effective than in the past in drawing trade from non-metropolitan areas.

Title: The Marketing Strategy of Planned Visual Communications
Affiliations: New York industrial design firm Gerald Stahl Associates, Hercules Powder, the 3M Company, U. S. Plywood, Yale & Towne, and Atlantic Refining.
Abstract: Frequently misrepresented, the concept of “corporate identity” is misunderstood by many marketing executives. This brief article defines the subject, details the concrete techniques involved, and outlines the realistic marketing benefits that company management can expect from a controlled plan of Visual Communications.

Title: Why Kill the Passenger Train?
Affiliations: School of Business at Northwestern University.
Abstract: Is the passenger train getting a “fair break” in the U.S. travel market? No, says the author of this article, an expert on transportation. He charges that railroad passenger-service losses have long been exaggerated by obsolete accounting rules of the Interstate Commerce Commission. However, some railroads that refuse to be deluded by “phantom” bookkeeping deficits are successfully marketing travel by train. If others would do likewise, the author points out, the results would be profitable both to the railroads and their customers.

Title: Albert Wesley Frey
Questionable Correlates for Automobile Shopping Behavior
Abstract: This is a three-fold reply to an earlier article in the JOURNAL OF MARKETING dealing with automobile shopping behavior. The present author feels that there was a failure to consider the type of measurement employed in the basic statistic.

Title: Rejoinders, Commentaries, and Specialized Articles Sales Promotion Effectiveness can be Measured
Affiliations: University of Illinois; McCann-Erickson's research affiliate
Abstract: John H. Weber argued in a recent issue of the JOURNAL OF MARKETING that the role of sales promotion in making sales cannot be measured quantitatively, because there are too many unknowns in the market place. He contended that general economic conditions affect consumer response to promotion in unknown, unmeasurable, and unpredictable ways; and he made the same point for local market conditions, competitive reactions, and intra-company factors. The present author takes issue with Weber's views—he asserts that the effectiveness of sales promotion activities can indeed be determined, and that experimental methods can be utilized.

Title: Sales Promotion Effectiveness Can Be Measured
Abstract: John H. Weber argued in a recent issue of the JOURNAL OF MARKETING that the role of sales promotion in making sales cannot be measured quantitatively, because there are too many unknowns in the market place. He contended that general economic conditions affect consumer response to promotion in unknown, unmeasurable, and unpredictable ways; and he made the same point for local market conditions, competitive reactions, and intra-company factors. The present author takes issue with Weber's views-he asserts that the effectiveness of sales promotion activities can indeed be determined, and that experimental methods can be utilized.

Title: Fringe Benefits or Salary?
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Industrial Management, University of Oregon
Abstract: Is management wasting a large portion of its payroll in unnecessary payments? Is it time to evaluate incentive systems for salaried employees in broader terms than cash payments alone? A first step is to find out how important “fringe benefits” or nonsalary compensation plans are in the minds of employees. The author reports on a study carried out to answer this and related questions.

Title: Financial Assistance for Graduate Students in Marketing, 1963–1964
Abstract: Here is a picture of the financial assistance available during 1963–1964 at leading schools of business throughout the U.S.A. for graduate students in marketing. There were 100 institutions that furnished detailed information for this second annual survey of financial aid — the first survey was summarized in the October, 1962. JOURNAL OF MARKETING.

Title: American Marketing Association Membership in 1963
Affiliations: Vice President of Elrick and Lavidge, Inc
Abstract: What are the characteristics of members of the American Marketing Association? How many members are there? When did they join? In which industries do they work? What are their job functions and titles? What changes currently are taking place within the AMA? This articles gives the answer.

Title: Why a Marketing Research Code of Ethics?
Abstract: Obtaining consumer opinions through organized marketing research is essential to modern marketing. But this implies fairness to consumers, and not abuse of their confidence. The Marketing Research Code of Ethics approved by the American Marketing Association spells out minimum ethical standards for researchers.

Title: Marketing in South Africa
Authors: Hugh G. Wales, F. F. Winklé, C. Bak
Affiliations: College of Commerce and Business Administration of the University of Illinois; Senior Lecturer in Business Economics at the University of South Africa, Pretoria, South Africa; Senior Lecturer in Business Economics at the University of South Africa
Abstract: The misconceptions about the economic, political, and social situations in Africa are numerous and complex. Among the developing and mature nations of Africa such as South Africa there are a number of diverse elements which range from the most primitive conditions to the modern technologies of the space age. Within this framework, this article briefly describes the marketing structure of the Republic of South Africa and the potentialities which exist for knowledgable executives in international and domestic trade.

Title: The use of Mathematical Models in Marketing
Abstract: Marketing executives and mathematicians have joined forces in a search for improved decision models to handle such problems as new-product development, media selection, retail inventory control, and size of sales force. The author of this article explains and illustrates those operations research models which hold the greatest promise in the marketing area.

Title: Marketing Government Surplus Property
Affiliations: Office of Supply Management in the headquarters of the General Services Administration in Washington, D.C
Abstract: Modern marketing techniques are now being used by the federal government in order to increase the return on its sales of surplus property. The author presents a general review of the government's sales practices, as carried out by the agency chiefly responsible for disposing of surplus property.

Title: The Consumer Speaks
Affiliations: Executive Vice-President and a Director of A. C. Nielsen Company
Abstract: Is Mrs. Consumer a satisfied grocery store customer? Can she get the specific brands, sizes, and colors she wants? What does she do when the brand, size, or color is out of stock—does she accept a substitute, or defer purchase until the next shopping trip? This article—based on a survey by the A. C. Nielsen Company, the results of which were presented at the 1962 annual meeting of the Grocery Manufacturers of America—discusses the potential loss of business to manufacturers and retail stores brought about by out-of-stock at the store level.

Title: Standardization of Advertising for Western Europe
Affiliations: Head of the international marketing consultancy of Victor Bossart and Associates, Zurich, Switzerland
Abstract: This article presents the principal factors pro and con as to the growth of standardized advertising practices in Western Europe. The author's presentations to the Fourth Congress of the International Advertising Association in Madrid in September, 1961, and to the Indiana University Second International Seminar on Marketing Management in Stresa, Italy, in July, 1962, have been brought up to date for readers of the JOURNAL OF MARKETING.

Title: The Products Liability Problem
Affiliations: The Lawyers Cooperative Publishing Company, Rochester, New York
Abstract: The problem of fixing legal responsibility for product-caused injury or death comes before today's courts with increasing frequency. American courts have begun to look not merely at the product itself and the harm caused, but also at the way in which the product was advertised and especially how it was described in the advertising. It is implied, therefore, that improper advertising can be the CAUSE of injury. And this means that both advertising agencies and advertisers have serious moral and legal responsibilities to see to it that this does not happen.

Title: Is Advertising Believability Really Important?
Affiliations: Manager of Research Development for Leo Burnett Company, and a Lecturer in the Evening Division of Northwestern University
Abstract: Most advertisers feel that to be effective, each advertisement must be noted, understood, and believed. Dr. Maloney draws upon a broad research background to demonstrate that an advertisement can be effective without being completely believed!

U. S. Consumption of Frozen Foods
Affiliations: Department of the Reuben H. Donnelley Telephone Directory Company, Division of Dun & Bradstreet.
Abstract: What figures are correct for U. S. consumption of frozen foods? The author provides figures different from some previously published.

Title: Can Refusals by Respondents be Decreased?
Authors: William P. Dommermuth, Philip R. Cateora
Affiliations: Assistant Professor of Marketing Administration at The University of Texas.; Assistant Professor of Marketing at the University of Southern California.
Abstract: Accuracy in consumer surveys can be influenced greatly by the degree to which the interviewer is “accepted” by the persons he seeks to question. Can the refusal rate be cut and the degree of acceptance increased if respondents are contacted by letter or phone before the interviewer's visit? The authors report on an experiment designed to answer this question.

Title: The Use of ROI in Sales Management
Affiliations: Professor and Area Chairman, Accounting and Taxation, at the Graduate School of Business, New York University.
Abstract: The shift in emphasis from sales volume to profitability as a measure of field sales management marked a real forward step in marketing management. One further step is necessary. The measure of effectiveness of business management should be return on investment (ROI), and not merely sales volume produced or profits as a percentage of sales. The field sales manager should be evaluated on the return on investment he produces in his segment of the business. The author believes that attention to ROI will not only result in harmonizing the objectives of the field sales organization with the over-all objective of the company, but will also equip field sales management with an effective businessman's tool for decision making.

Title: Census Distortions of Food Broker Sales
Affiliations: Marketing and a Ph.D. in Business from the University of Illinois
Abstract: Because of the Census Bureau's methods of tabulating, there are distortions with respect to sales by food brokers. These affect Census of Business data. What can be done to improve methods of tabulation? This is a matter of concern to all marketing men.

Title: What Are “Commodities of like Grade and Quality”?
Affiliations: Lecturer in Marketing in the School of Business Administration at the State University of New York at Buffalo
Abstract: The U. S. Supreme Court was never more correct than in saying that “precision of expression is not an outstanding characteristic of the Robinson-Patman Act.” This article shows the varied interpretations given by the FTC to one section of the Act, dealing with “commodities of like grade and quality.” The author also shows how the phrase “like grade and quality” may be given sharper and less ambiguous meaning.

Title: The Service Revolution
Affiliations: Professor of Business at San Francisco State College and Coordinator of the Graduate Program.
Abstract: Are we running out of physical-goods markets? The author shows how a large and growing market for commodities lies in the development of service systems.

Title: What Could Nonexposure Tell the TV Advertiser?
Authors: Irwin M. Towers, Leo A. Goodman, Hans Zeisel
Affiliations: Columbia University, and was a national winner of the Affiliated Advertising Agency Network Scholarship; Professor of Statistics and Sociology at the University of Chicago; Zeisel is Professor of Law and Sociology at the University of Chicago Law School
Abstract: This is a critique of the usual techniques used to gauge the effectiveness of TV advertising. Also, a new TV-testing method is proposed, aimed at providing more valid results. A controlled experiment, conducted in a realistic setting, with nonexposure to television controlled, forms the basis of this method.

Title: Marketing in Finland
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Advertising, University of Rhode Island
Abstract: Many readers will be surprised to learn of the timely marketing practices and institutions which characterize the small nation of Finland. Its “Americana” marketing appearance, exemplified by planned shopping centers, television advertising, and self-service stores seems incongruous with a common border with the Soviet Union. Wholesaling, retailing, and advertising are some of the areas included in this firsthand report of Finnish marketing.

Title: How to Evaluate Field Sales Promotion
Affiliations: B.A. degree from the University of Cincinnati where he was a member of Phi Beta Kappa, and an M.B.A. degree from the Harvard Graduate School of Business Administration where he was a Baker Scholar.
Abstract: Of the many weapons in the modern marketer's arsenal, sales promotion methods often are used blindly. This article diagnoses this situation, and includes a standard evaluation form for use in appraising field promotions.

Title: Patterns behind “Income Refusals”
Affiliations: Wayne State University, Mr. Skelton has been Vice President of the Detroit Chapter of the American Marketing Association
Abstract: Although income is an important variable in assessing marketing behavior, information about income is difficult to obtain through survey research. This article examines refusals to income questions for significant patterns. Ways to reduce nonresponses are also suggested.

Title: The Public Relations of Interviewing
Affiliations: Colby College, Mr. Schwartz has an M.S. degree in journalism from Northwestern University.
Abstract: The relationships between interviewers and prospective respondents are crucial to the success of every marketing research project. Based on the results from a recent study, this article explores some approaches to improving these relationships.

Title: How Practical is the Media Model?
Affiliations: Manager of the Media Department of Young & Rubicam, Inc., New York.
Abstract: This article is a fitting conclusion to the preceding one, “Practical Media Decisions and the Computer,” by William T. Moran. Mr. St. Georges deals with the stages by which media decision makers will realize the potential of the computerized media decision model. He raises serious questions about the requirements and potential sources of necessary data, but shows why the model eventually will enhance rather than inhibit media judgment and creativity.

Title: Practical Media Decisions and the Computer
Affiliations: Manager of the Research Department at Young & Rubicam, Inc., New York.
Abstract: Of the variety of new computer applications, the most important is the development of decision models for media selection. This article discusses the development of decision models in general, the development of a practical media decision model which grew out of disillusionment with linear programing, the ways that this model's requirements for new data are being met, and the implications of the model for the future of the advertising business. After reading this article, read the succeeding one, “How Practical Is the Media Model?” by Joseph St. Georges (pp. 31–33).

Title: How Not to Do Consumer Research
Authors: J. Stevens Stock, Barbara K. Auerbach
Affiliations: Director of Research of McCann-Erickson in Chicago, and then Vice President of Alfred Politz Research, Inc., New York.; Director of Research at J. Stevens Stock Research Co. A graduate of Radcliffe College, Miss Auerbach received her M.A. in Sociology from New York University.
Abstract: People often seek their friends' opinions about the quality of goods and services before buying. But should a collection of opinions be offered to the public as apparently scientific proof of quality? The marketing researcher assumes particular responsibility when he attempts to use public opinion as a method of evaluating products and services for the buying public. In this discussion of some of the difficulties involved in consumer research, the authors use a widely-read CONSUMER REPORTS magazine survey as an example.

Title: An Economist Defends Advertising
Affiliations: Professor of Economics at Arizona State University.
Abstract: In this article an economist presents a highly critical review of a standard economic attack on the advertising industry. He pinpoints errors in economic analysis, and shows how the advertising industry is in an excellent position for a counterattack. In this connection, see “Marketing's Challenge to Economists,” by Quentin L. Coons, pp. 11–15.

Title: Marketing's Challenge to Economics
Affiliations: Harvard College (1925) and the Harvard Graduate School of Business Administration (1928)
Abstract: Clearly recognized in the President's 1962 Economic Report to Congress is the fact that “faster economic growth in the United States requires, above all, EXPANSION OF DEMAND.” But most academic economists remain critical, ignoring or denying the contributions of creative marketing to a dynamic economy and questioning marketing's value as a progressive social force. Read what Quentin L. Coons has to say to these economists. Also see “An Economist Defends Advertising,” by John W. Lowe, pp. 16–19.

Title: A Pioneering Experiment in Assessing Advertising Effectiveness
Abstract: According to this article, there are only two basic dimensions to the effectiveness of advertising: (1) size of audience, and (2) depth of impact. The advertising industry has been spending most of its research dollars in measuring the audience component, with the result that we can now measure this dimension reasonably well. Dr. Coffin believes it is now time to spend more dollars in assessing the dimension of impact—for it is this area which, for the future, promises the greatest improvement in advertising evaluation and sound media comparisons.

Title: Henry J. Kaiser
What Models in Marketing?
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration at Michigan State University
Abstract: This is a 5-point rejoinder to the previous article, pp. 70–73.

Title: Real Models in Marketing, or Phony Games?
Affiliations: University of Tulsa and Case Institute of Technology, Drexel Institute of Technology, and Roosevelt University
Abstract: Do mathematical models have a role to play in marketing? Do we now have models to offer for business decision? Should the emphasis be on the mathematics, or on the models? Here are some provocative ideas.

Title: The Jantzen Method of Short-Range Forecasting
Affiliations: School of Business, University of Oregon
Abstract: Sales forecasting by ratio estimation has produced good results for Jantzen Inc. The method is represented here, with the thought that it might be used by other business firms where suitable records are available.

Title: A Closer Look at Operations Research
Affiliations: Division of Cresap, Behr-Manning Co. of Troy, New York
Abstract: Until recently a novelty in the world of business, Operations Research is still something of a mystery to most people. Although the author of this article does not claim to dispel this mystery completely, he does lighten it considerably.

Title: Are Automobile Purchasers Dissonant Consumers?
Affiliations: University of Michigan Graduate School of Business Administration, University of Illinois
Abstract: Are there really “dissonant consumers”—that is, consumers beset with doubt after a purchase that they have made the correct choice? The author examines this question, using the findings of his study of new automobile owners; and he discusses the issue of the advertiser's responsibility to the recent purchaser.

Title: The Breakthrough in Sales Forecasting
Affiliations: Scovill Manufacturing Company, Waterbury, Connecticut, University of Notre Dame and Syracuse University
Abstract: The techniques described in this article show how time series analysis can be used in sales forecasting. For several years experiments have been conducted in using time series analysis in forecasting sales at the Scovill Manufacturing Company, and considerable empirical data have been assembled. The techniques for anticipating sales, developed through these experiments, are described here.

Title: Relating Company Markets to SIC
Affiliations: Economic and Marketing Analysis, Harvard College, New York University.
Abstract: Even where marketing statistics are available by 4-digit Standard Industrial Classification, their usefulness as an indicator of market potential is limited until the relationship beween a special company market and the SIC has been clearly defined. A useful approach to the problem of defining this relationship is to begin with the product, as shown in this article.

Title: Competent Retail Trainees—Where Are They ?
Affiliations: De Paul University, University of Minnesota.
Abstract: Retailers have long complained about their inability to attract and retain employes with executive potenial. Here are some new avenues of approach.

Title: What is Meant by Franchise Selling?
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, College of Business Administration, University of Iowa, University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: Too often cooperatives and wholesaler-sponsored chains are described as franchise selling. This marketing man shows how voluntary groups and franchise selling are sufficiently different that these terms should be recognized as distinct concepts.

Title: Interviewer Bias in Selecting Households
Authors: Roy E. Garter, Verling C. Troldahl, R. Smith Schuneman
Affiliations: Research Division of the University of Minnesota School of Journalism, School of Journalism and Institute for Research in Social Science at the University of North Carolina, Stanford University; Michigan State University, Division at the University of Minnesota.; University of Minnesota and Ohio University
Abstract: The question raised in this article is: To what extent will noninterviewers be able to identify the households which interviewers themselves chose or rejected when they were assigned sex and age quotas in small block clusters? Apparently serious biases may be introduced when interviewers are briefed to use random-type methods in proceeding through an area.

Title: The Changing Australian Food Industry
Affiliations: University of New England, Armidale, N.S.W., Australia; Southern Illinois University, Department of Agricultural Industries
Abstract: Food marketing “down under” increasingly is becoming Americanized. Utilizing business arrangements which range from licensing agreements to wholly owned subsidiaries, American food firms are invading the Australian market with a plethora of products. Here is an up-to-date description of the marketing techniques that are evolving.

Title: Food Marketing in Western Europe Today
Affiliations: Agricultural Economics Research Institute, Oxford University, and University of California
Abstract: Food trade in Europe is undergoing many changes; and both retailers and investors seem to be getting confidence in self-service supermarkets, prepackaging, frozen foods, and similar developments. But what about public opinion? What about suitable suppliers and managers? This article gives some answers to these and related questions.

Title: A Low-Cost Method for Identifying TV Audiences
Affiliations: The Pulse, Inc., marketing research company, Columbia University; The Pulse, Inc., New York University
Abstract: The high costs of television make it increasingly important that TV commercials appear on programs which reach the right prospects for the advertised products and for isolating program audiences in large numbers for subsequent analysis of characteristics. The authors believe that a method now exists. Their article describes a method to expand the sample, without expanding cost unduly, and without affecting reliability of data obtained.

Title: Mass Marketing and Warranty Liability
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration at The University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, University of Michigan
Abstract: How do decisions by marketing managers and advertising executives influence court decisions pertaining to the law of products liability? Manufacturers face an increasing number of damage claims from consumers, and recent cases modifying the rules of substantive law enhance a plaintiff's prospect of successful suit. The author explains why the law of products liability continues to develop and expand.

Title: The Federal Trade Commission of the 1960s
Abstract: What are some of the recent changes in procedures of the Federal Trade Commission? And how is the FTC giving additional protection against unfair business practices? An FTC spokesman gives the answers.

Alpha Kappa PSI Foundation Award
Next Sales Meeting—Try a Game
Affiliations: Business Administration, University of California, Berkeley, Pennsylvania's Wharton School, San Francisco State College
Abstract: Here is an account of a business game designed to keep interest at a high pitch, and at the same time highlight a critical sales management problem. No computer installation is required; and simple rules describe the manner in which this effective sales training device may be used.

Title: Indirect Price Discrimination and Robinson-Patman
Affiliations: University of Kentucky. Cornell University's Graduate School of Business, Indiana University
Abstract: This article is a case study of how one firm unwillingly violated Section 2(d) of the Robinson-Patman Act by merely participating in a cooperative advertising plan. It shows that the Federal Trade Commission's strict interpretation of the law's language can frustrate innovation in marketing strategy.

Title: A Probability Model for Early Prediction of New Product Market Success
Abstract: This article shows the application of a simple probability model to one aspect of the early prediction of new product success. The model is tested by comparing a long-run predicted proportion of Chicago families who would be expected to buy a particular new product during a bimonthly period with the actual proportions buying since introduction.

Title: Identifying Likely Sales Prospects
Affiliations: Corporation in Princeton, New Jersey. Fordham University.; Research Professor of Economics University of Illinois
Abstract: This article describes a “user-nomination” research methodology for identifying nonusers of a product or service. The case history describing the technique is from a study by Opinion Research Corporation.

Title: What about Reader Service Cards?
Authors: W. J. E. Crissy, Gary A. Marple
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Transportation Administration at Michigan State University.; Department of Marketing and Transportation Administration at Michigan State University. A graduate of Drake University, Michigan State University.
Abstract: Is the reader service card an effective aid to marketing effort? Advertisers, advertising agencies, inquiry users, and publishers have different views regarding this question. This article presents those views, as well as some evidence on effectiveness.

Title: Retail Strategy and the Classification of Consumer Goods
Affiliations: University of California, Berkeley. University of Colorado and Northwestern University. School of Industrial Management, M.I.T.
Abstract: What guides are available to aid the retailer in developing his marketing strategy? The author shows how the traditional concepts of shopping, convenience, and specialty goods may be updated and integrated with the idea of patronage motives, and how they provide the retailer with a new means of evaluating his strategy.

Title: “Normal” Business Behavior and the Justice Department
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles. University of Washington, University of California.
Abstract: Antitrust indictments against business firms often appear to businessmen and the community to represent an unfair attack on normal business behavior by an “anti-business” arm of the government. The author examines the rationale for the enforcement of proscriptions against one form of business activity—price fixing—and concludes that where such behavior is concerned, considerations of “fairness” or “normality” can have no bearing.

Title: A Model for Marketing Programing
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business at Indiana University.
Abstract: The mix concept is a marketing fact of life, but it has not produced for the marketing manager. The author questions the usefulness of the conventional mix concept and suggests an alternative approach to marketing program design.

Title: The Future of Discounting
Authors: William R. Davidson, Alton F. Doody
Abstract: There is much speculation about the discount house being the “store of the future,” capable of revolutionizing all or a large part of retailing. This article evaluates the competitive significance of discounting and places it within a realistic marketing perspective.

Title: Retailing in Great Britain
Affiliations: Department at Northwestern University; Ruthrauff and Ryan, Ltd.
Abstract: How different is retailing in Great Britain from retailing in the United States? How can the differences be explained? What can be predicted for British retailing? These are the questions answered in this article.

Title: The Acceleration Effect in Forecasting Industrial Shipments
Authors: Alfred A. Kuehn, Ralph L. Day
Affiliations: Graduate School of Industrial Administration, Carnegie Institute of Technology; Department of Marketing Administration, University of Texas, University of North Carolina.
Abstract: The level of consumption of many industrial products is closely related to the general level of industrial activity. Yet forecasts of industrial activity are generally more accurate than forecasts of factory shipments for a particular industry. A method is presented for deriving better forecasts of manufacturers' sales from projections of general industrial activity by systematic analysis of inventory behavior at all levels of distribution.

Title: Pretesting Advertising with the Differential Attitude Technique
Affiliations: Psychology Department of University College, Rutgers University.
Abstract: The results obtained with the advertising pretest procedure presented in this article indicate that the differential effect on readers' attitudes of print ads (and probably other types of advertising as well) can be satisfactorily measured by a fairly simple scalar technique. Thus, an ad can be evaluated prior to publication in terms of its impact on attitudes rather than in terms of the recall of specific aspects of the ad.

Title: Can Results of Sales Promotion be Predicted?
Affiliations: College of Agriculture of the University of Idaho, University of Minnesota, University of Oregon
Abstract: Can the part that promotion plays in making sales be quantitatively measured and predicted for the future? This author offers evidence that conditions in the marketplace are so unknown and change so quickly that it is almost impossible to measure all in the course of an experiment, let alone try to duplicate them for future prediction.

Title: Bayesian Decision Theory in Pricing Strategy
Affiliations: Department of the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School.
Abstract: Both this article and the preceding one by Harry V. Roberts on “Bayesian Statistics in Marketing” (pp. 1–4) show that Bayesian statistics is a new and potentially powerful tool for systematically working with management judgments. The present article by Paul E. Green shows how this approach can be used in the area of pricing analysis.

Title: Bayesian Statistics in Marketing
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business at the University of Chicago
Abstract: Bayesian statistics points the way to an articulation of business judgment and statistical research in approaching marketing problems. We have always known that neither executive nor statistician is sufficient in himself, but now for the first time we have formal tools that show that the two can be brought closer together. This article shows how this may be accomplished. Also, see the succeeding article, “Bayesian Decision Theory in Pricing Strategy,” by Paul E. Green, pp. 5–14.

Title: George H. Gallup
Correlates of Automobile Shopping Behavior
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business, University of Chicago
Abstract: The kinds of shopping behavior exhibited by automobile purchasers have implications for both advertising and selling strategy. This article illustrates a methodology for studying shopping deportment and suggests possible hypotheses about the importance of this kind of analysis.

Title: Pre-Case Analysis for Students
Abstract: Most students jump to recommendations and conclusions for cases almost before they have finished reading them for the first time. This article describes a way of forcing marketing students to do more analysis before preparing a formal case report.

Title: Marketing Laws and Marketing Strategy
Abstract: If decisions of marketing managers are to be influenced by predictions based on theoretical models, it is important that the assumptions in the models be accurate. Marketeers must reformulate concepts in such models to make them empirically meaningful, as the author of this article shows.

Title: Automated Grocery Shopping
Affiliations: University of Western Ontario; University of Illinois
Abstract: Automatic vending has come to hold equal fascination for the marketing practitioner, the academic theorist, and the average consumer. Unfortunately, it has also been the recipient of more than its share of “blue-sky” prognoses. This article gives the results of an interesting experiment in grocery vending conducted by a midwestern supermarket chain.

Title: Current Shifts in Electrical Wholesaling
Affiliations: Northwestern University Medill School of Journalism
Abstract: Established marketing institutions and practices are undergoing changes. The wholesaler in particular is under pressure; and he is striving to improve his position, as this article shows.

Title: The Roots of Large Scale Retailing
Affiliations: School of Business at the University of Toronto
Abstract: For a century, retailing has been leavened by a succession of large scale retailers—the department store, the mail order house, the chain store, the supermarket, and the discount house. What are the common, underlying reasons for their emergence? Will the pattern continue? Here is a critical answer.

Title: Hidden Errors in Survey Data
Affiliations: Rutgers University, Developmental Research Unit in the Research Department of Benton & Bowles, Inc; Rutgers University
Abstract: How accurately do respondents report in marketing research surveys? This study shows that survey results can be correct for a total sample, even when many individuals have not reported accurately. But the study also shows that seemingly correct results sometimes conceal a bias which leads to false conclusions.

Title: New Products Need Special Management
Abstract: Believing that most companies do not go after new products effectively, the author deals with what is wrong and what to do about it. Of special interest is the theme that the responsibility for new products should not rest with the marketing function.

Title: Ferment in Marketing's Oldest Area
Affiliations: College of Commerce and Administration of The Ohio State University

Title: Personal Interviews or Mail Panels?
Affiliations: College of Commerce of the University of Illinois
Abstract: Blind allegiance to a particular marketing research technique is frequently the cause of survey inefficiency. According to Mr. O'Dell, the never deviating adherence of many practitioners to the mail panel or a rigorous probability sample leads to waste and excessively costly survey data. He presents some new, objective findings here, to aid the researcher in selecting the most efficient data-gathering method.

Title: Financial Assistance for Graduate Students in Marketing
Abstract: For the first time, graduate students in marketing have available a summarized picture of the financial assistance available during 1962–1963 at leading business schools throughout the country. The fact that 68 institutions furnished detailed information for this first survey of financial aid points up the importance of providing this service for people interested in graduate work in the marketing field.

Title: Are There Fashion Cycles in Creative Advertising?
Authors: William T. Kelley, Robert G. Duke
Affiliations: Wharton School of Finance and Commerce; Benton & Bowles, Inc., New York
Abstract: It has often been alleged that advertising people are faddists, that they “jump on the bandwagon” whenever a new creative idea comes along. By careful statistical analysis of advertising formats that have appeared in two consumer magazines, the authors have tested the validity of this charge.

Title: Advertising and Social Values
Affiliations: Drury College; Massachusetts Institute of Technology School of Industrial Management
Abstract: This article was written independently of the one preceding, by Colston E. Warne. The point that authors Petit and Zakon are making is that advertising is a bulwark rather than a threat to our existing values. They maintain that critics of advertising who say that it violates the American value system are in reality criticizing the American value system itself.

Title: Advertising—A Critic's View
Abstract: Has advertising degenerated into wasteful and sometimes deceptive promotion of brand rivalry? Since the author of the present article says, “Yes,” it might be well to point out that an old-fashioned but still valid tenet is that a good marketing man must always try to learn about and understand another person's point of view. In this article, originally presented at the 1961 Boston Conference on Distribution (Colston E. Warne, “Advertising—A Critic's View,” Boston, International Marketing Institute, 1961, pp. 61–65), the author maintains that present-day advertising is featuring the irrational and the irrelevant, and is often employed as a means of consumer manipulation. For a different point of view, see the article that follows this one.

Title: Should Salesmen's Compensation be Geared to Profits?
Authors: Ralph L. Day, Peter D. Bennett
Abstract: Do most sales managers try to maximize sales volume to the detriment of profits? The authors do not think so. Methods are proposed for shifting incentives from sales volume to profits through better utilization of data available from electronic data processing systems.

Title: Formal Reasoning and Marketing Strategy
Affiliations: School of Commerce and Business Administration, University of Alabama
Abstract: Some serious marketing theorists are attempting to use formal reasoning in creating marketing programs. This article surveys the new methods developed by formalists. The implications of this new approach are important to all marketing executives and researchers.

Title: Marketing Articles in Review

Authors: Kenneth J. Curran, Marshall C. Howard, Charles E. Stonier, Ray O. Werner
Affiliations: Department of Economics Colorado College; University of Massachusetts; Hofstra College; Colorado College
Abstract: The most important recent developments in the legal framework within which marketing must function are reported under the topical outline presented below. More detailed information about individual items maybe obtained by reference to the source cited for each case. References to CCH are to the Commerce Clearing House Trade Regulation Reporter.

Title: Legal Developments in Marketing
The Computer and the Marketing Man
Leaders in Marketing
Authors: Arthur C. Nielsen, James Playsted Wood

Title: Arthur C. Nielsen
More “Why” about Portfolio Tests
Why Aren't Portfolio Tests Here to Stay?
Abstract: The purpose of this article is to comment on certain aspects of portfolio tests, with particular reference to John C. Maloney's article in the JOURNAL OF MARKETING (July, 1961). The comments are organized in terms of how a portfolio test should perform to be of maximal value, pointing up certain areas of needed research.

Title: A Survey of Marketing Games
Authors: J. F. McRaith, Charles R. Goeldner, Robert Ferber
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, San Fernando Valley State College; Division of Business and Economics at San Fernando Valley State College; University of Illinois
Abstract: Most people in marketing have had no contact with marketing games, and many are not even aware of them. The purpose here is to provide an illustrative list of the games available to marketing executives and educators.

Title: The Group Depth Interview
Affiliations: Research Development with National Analysts, Inc.
Abstract: “Discussion panels,” “respondent-oriented interviews,” “consumer conferences,” and “focused group interviews” have enjoyed increasing popularity in attempting to solve marketing problems. This article describes the mechanics of conducting group interviews and also some of its consequences. The title of the article, “The Group Depth Interview,” reflects a situation in which information is sought from a number of interacting individuals at the same time, using a combination of probing and direct-inquiry techniques.

Title: Watch for those Unseen Variables
Abstract: There are a number of subtle but important variables which frequently go uncontrolled in marketing surveys. The present study clearly illustrates that when such “unseen” variables are neglected, research findings may be influenced in a manner which is difficult, or even impossible, to predict.

Title: How Extensive the Planning and Development Program?
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, DePaul University, Chicago
Abstract: Cut short the planning and development program — and risk a serious mistake? Or carry it out more fully—and risk delay of entry into the market? Seven factors are suggested which should influence the executive in managing his product-planning and development program.

Title: Pricing to Gain Wholesalers’ Selling Support
Affiliations: The University of Michigan School of Business Administration
Abstract: Can a manufacturer do anything to increase the selling effort expended by his wholesalers? Is greater emphasis on direct sale the only way to gain greater promotional activity at wholesale levels? The author shows that the manufacturer through his pricing policies may exert an important influence on wholesaler willingness and ability to sell.

Title: Automobiles by the Pound
Authors: Robert J. Holloway, Donald J. Hempel
Affiliations: University of Minnesota; Instructor in the School of Business Administration at the University of Minnesota
Abstract: Although you may never purchase an automobile on a per pound basis, you will be intrigued with the relationship between weight and price described in this article.

Title: The Marketing Oriented Technical Product Development Program
Affiliations: Marketing Research Department, the Nestle Co., Inc.
Abstract: Management has had to endorse huge investment spending programs on new product development to insure market position and profits for the future. This places a tremendous burden upon the New Product Department. This article shows why the responsibilities for communicating and administering the technical development phases should be assigned to the central Marketing Research Department.

Title: Discount Houses in Australia and Mexico
Abstract: The discount house is the latest American marketing innovation to be exported and to be met with the cry “It can't happen here.” In an article in the April, 1962, JOURNAL OF MARKETING, the author generalized that marketing activities that would work in the United States would usually work in Australia. Here he examines the discount house against the Australia marketing scene and in Mexico, another market which has shown some willingness to accept American marketing ideas but not without resistance.

Title: Suppliers, Retailers, and Shelf Space
Affiliations: Department of Political and Economic Science, The Royal Military College of Canada, Kingston, Canada
Abstract: There are a number of ways of looking at the functions of the retailer … and the author of this article would like to regard him as a seller of space to suppliers. This is a helpful approach in analyzing the relationship between the manufacturers of consumer goods, particularly of the convenience type, and the retailers of these goods.

Title: The Role of the Marketing Staff
Affiliations: J. Walter Thompson Company, New York
Abstract: Business management is increasingly dependent upon marketing to gain enduring competitive advantage. This article describes the rich opportunities for success presented by a change in the approach to marketing staff work and acquisition of professional personnel for it.

Title: Marketing to the Navy
Affiliations: U.S. Naval Weapons Plant, Washington, D.C.
Abstract: Marketing portrays the manner in which the military term logistic requirement, is translated into business usage as market. Using the Navy as an example, the entire purchase cycle is outlined. This is believed to be the first time the military market has been covered from so broad a view. The article is also unusual in being written by a “customer.”

Title: Protect your Trademark by Proper Usage
Abstract: The common names of many well-known products once were trademarks that belonged to particular manufacturers. But these trademarks passed into the language as generic terms because they were, in a sense, too successful. This article shows why trademarks become generic and describes several different methods which may be used, singly or in combination, to avoid this result.

Title: Decision Theory and Marketing Management
Authors: Robert D. Buzzell, Charles C. Slater
Affiliations: Graduate School of Business Administration, Harvard University; Marketing Research of Omar
Abstract: This article discusses three topics: a brief summary of decision theory as a tool of marketing management; a description of the nature and sources of wholesale bakers’ present marketing problems; and a step-by-step account of the use of decision theory in the analysis of one of these problems.

Title: Marketing under Attack
Authors: D. Beryl Manischewitz, John A. Stuart
Affiliations: The B. Manischewitz Company, Newark, N. J.; Department of the National Association of Manufacturers
Abstract: Year by year, almost day by day, the flow of criticism reflecting upon the value of marketing concepts appears to be intensifying. The question is — what posture should “Organized Marketing” properly assume in the situation? The authors offer a program under which both the intellectual and activist elements of marketing may work to solve their problems.
